docs.t: The trigger
docs.x: A communications agency with 80 employees has no clearance project. It has the usual: 300 hoodies and 2,400 notebooks with the old logo after a rebrand, 15 monitors from a refresh, shelves and chairs from a dissolved meeting room, a coffee machine, 60 roll-up banners after the trade-show season. None of it is worth a collection by a logistics partner. Until now it went to the basement, then to the skip, or a colleague took it home. The trigger: a client asked for a VSME sustainability record in a pitch. The agency had intentions but no numbers. “We donated every year, somehow. We could prove none of it.” - Office Manager, communications agency
docs.p: Twelve Small Donations a Year: Seed for an Agency

docs.t: The process
docs.x: The agency took the Seed subscription with twelve matches a year. Two users, one onboarding call, then it ran on the side: Listing in ten minutes: photo, quantity, condition - the AI Copilot writes the rest: listing copy, impact copy, later the social-media impact card. Personally coordinated matching: the monitors went in two lots to a neighbourhood centre and an education provider, the hoodies to a homeless service, the shelves to a clothing bank, the roll-ups to a sports club for its stand. Handover by the agency: recipients collected, or a colleague dropped by on the way home. No logistics partner, no collection costs. Handover confirmed in the dashboard. The newsletter as trigger: three of the eleven matches happened the other way round - an NGO posted a need in the weekly needs newsletter, and the agency had it in the basement.
docs.p: Twelve Small Donations a Year: Seed for an Agency

docs.t: The honest maths
docs.x: Almost nothing happens tax-wise: the second-hand value of the lots is small, VAT on it around €120 a year, the deduction recovers about a third. sur.plus prepares the donation certificates as far as possible; the recipient releases and countersigns them. The subscription costs €990 a year. Against that: around €900 in disposal, about 30 hours of internal time that used to go into enquiries and basement clear-outs - and the export in Voluntary Standard format the client wanted to see. “The pitch appendix ended up being one page from the dashboard. That was enough.” - Managing Director, communications agency
docs.p: Twelve Small Donations a Year: Seed for an Agency

docs.x: How a children’s clothing e-shop gives returns of limited saleability to clothing banks as a weekly lot - one condition class, one CSV, one collection day.

docs.t: How does an e-shop plug into sur.plus - without integration?
docs.x: Through one condition class at grading and a weekly CSV with item, quantity, condition and purchase value. One collection point per site, fixed collection days. A system integration only makes sense with several sites and is then part of an Enterprise offer.

docs.t: Does donating returns cost VAT?
docs.x: Yes. New goods are valued at purchase price when donated, goods of limited saleability at a documented discount, worthless goods at zero. sur.plus documents the condition per lot so the base holds up.

docs.x: How a children’s clothing e-shop gives returns of limited saleability to clothing banks as a weekly lot - one condition class at grading, one file on Friday, collection on Tuesday. Illustrative example. This scenario shows a typical trigger and the process the platform is built for. Real cases will replace these examples as soon as pilot partners release them.
docs.p: E-commerce Returns: the Weekly Lot as a Donation

docs.t: The trigger
docs.x: A children’s clothing e-shop with 45 employees takes in around 1,400 returns a week. Most go back to stock, some to the outlet. What remains is about 180 items a week that can no longer be sold at full price: opened packaging, missing tags, washed, last season. Until now: a collection box, a liquidator, and disposal when the liquidator declined. The destruction ban only applies to a shop this size from 2030. The trigger was different: marketing wanted to put “We destroy no returns” on the product pages. Under the new rules against greenwashing, that claim needs evidence. “The claim was written in a minute. The evidence behind it was not.” - Head of Returns, e-shop
docs.p: E-commerce Returns: the Weekly Lot as a Donation

docs.t: The process
docs.x: The decision is made where it is made anyway: at returns intake. The team added one class to grading - C: limited saleability, donate - with a one-page rule for what belongs in it. No ERP project, no interface. Friday: a CSV export from the returns system - item, quantity, size run, condition class, purchase value. Uploaded as the weekly lot. Effort: 20 minutes. Tuesday: collection at the collection point in the warehouse. Two clothing banks and a family centre in rotation, depending on reported needs and sizes. Feedback: what recipients cannot use (summer stock in November) flows back into the grading rule - the share of unusable items per lot fell from 18 to 6 percent.
docs.p: E-commerce Returns: the Weekly Lot as a Donation

docs.t: The honest maths
docs.x: New goods cost VAT when donated. For “limited saleability” half the purchase value is used: over twelve weeks that was around €1,850 in VAT, the deduction recovers around €550, net about minus €1,300. Against that: avoided handling and disposal costs of around €1,950 - and the evidence marketing needed. “I never believed donating would pay. It pays narrowly, and it is the only option where we can prove anything afterwards.” - Managing Director, e-shop
docs.p: E-commerce Returns: the Weekly Lot as a Donation

docs.t: The outcome after 12 weeks
docs.x: 2,160 Items in twelve weekly lots 3 Recipients: 2 clothing banks, 1 family centre ~700 Children clothed (recipients’ estimate) 2.2 t CO₂ avoided (GHG Protocol) −€1,300 Net tax effect (VAT on half the purchase value minus deduction) 20 min Internal effort per week Twelve-week pilot with go/no-go; then an ongoing offer for the site. The evidence pack documents offer, acceptance and handover per lot; donation certificates prepared by sur.plus as far as possible, released and countersigned by the recipient - per lot. The VAT base depends on the documented condition - agree it with your tax adviser. ← All case studies

docs.t: Insolvency: Tools and Building Materials Donated
docs.x: How an insolvency administrator donated a trade business’s remaining stock after the auction - clearance avoided, estate protected, file complete.

docs.t: May an insolvency administrator donate remaining stock?
docs.x: Realisation is the administrator’s call. If clearance costs more than a sale would bring in, a donation protects the estate - provided the decision is documented. sur.plus supplies the comparison, handover records and donation certificates for that file.

docs.t: How fast is a clearance via sur.plus?
docs.x: In the case above, 16 days from commission to warehouse handover. The fixed price is quoted before the start; collection runs through logistics partners at cost.

docs.t: One insolvency administrator, one warehouse full of tools
docs.x: How an insolvency administrator donated a trade business’s remaining stock after the auction - clearance costs avoided, the estate protected, everything documented for the final report. Illustrative example. This scenario shows a typical trigger and the process the platform is built for. Companies and recipients are deliberately unnamed; figures are illustrative and follow the Impact Calculator methodology (GHG Protocol, GIIN IRIS+, tax effect versus disposal). Real cases will replace these examples as soon as pilot partners release them.
docs.p: Insolvency: Tools and Building Materials Donated

docs.t: The trigger
docs.x: A plumbing and heating business with 40 employees is being wound up. The insolvency administrator has sold vehicles and large machinery through an auction house. What remains is what no bidder wanted: six workbenches, hand tools in 40 crates, warehouse racking, three pallets of tiles, pipes, fittings, insulation and twelve office workstations. Replacement value around €38,000, roughly six tonnes. The warehouse has to go back to the landlord in three weeks. The clearance quote: €7,800 - a liability of the estate that creditors would lose. “After the auction there is always a remainder. Until now the remainder meant: order a skip and pay the bill from the estate.” - Insolvency administrator
docs.p: Insolvency: Tools and Building Materials Donated

docs.t: The process
docs.x: The administrator commissioned a clearance project at a fixed price, quoted before the start and paid from the estate. His office listed the remaining stock in four lots with photos and quantities; matching was personally coordinated within the deadline. Workbenches and hand tools to an education provider’s training workshop and a repair café association. Tiles, pipes, fittings, insulation to a youth building project and a non-profit self-build housing project. Office workstations to the education provider for a second site. Logistics: two collection days, logistics partner at cost, €1,900. Handover record per lot.
docs.p: Insolvency: Tools and Building Materials Donated

docs.t: The honest maths
docs.x: In insolvency the donation deduction plays no role - there is no profit for it to reduce. What counts is the estate: €7,800 clearance avoided against €1,900 logistics, the fixed price and around €570 VAT on the second-hand value. For the final report everything sits in one file: the clearance quote, the comparison, the donation decision, handover records and donation certificates per recipient - prepared by sur.plus, released and countersigned by the recipient. “I need a justification for every euro out of the estate. This file is the justification.” - Insolvency administrator

docs.t: The trigger
docs.x: A consultancy with 520 employees replaces 400 laptops after four years. After inspection the ITAD partner buys back 280 devices - €95 on average, €26,600 in proceeds. For the remaining 120 there is no offer: older generation, casing damage, weak batteries. The inspection report marks them “no market”. The usual route would have been free take-back for recycling - working devices, shredded, no evidence. “The ITAD did its job. For 120 devices its job just wasn’t the answer.” - Head of IT, consultancy
docs.p: IT Refresh: 280 Laptops Sold, 120 Donated

docs.t: The process
docs.x: The head of IT listed the no-market lot on sur.plus - using the ITAD inspection report as the basis: serial numbers, condition per device, and the erasure certificates the ITAD had produced for all 400 devices anyway. One onboarding call, then personally coordinated matching. Four matches: two school associations for learning labs, a migration advice centre, a youth centre. All four needed devices for browser, office and learning platforms - the older generation is enough for that. Collection straight from the ITAD: the logistics partner collected the four sub-lots from the ITAD warehouse, no detour via the consultancy. Evidence per device: serial number, erasure certificate, recipient, handover record. For the data protection officer this was the decisive point.
docs.p: IT Refresh: 280 Laptops Sold, 120 Donated

docs.t: The honest maths
docs.x: A device without market value brings no tax advantage as a donation either. The second-hand value of the lot was around €3,600, attracting about €680 in VAT; the deduction recovers around €200. Net: about minus €480. Selling was clearly better financially for 280 devices - and that is exactly what the consultancy did. For the other 120 the only choice was disposal without evidence or donation with evidence. “We wanted to write in the sustainability report that no working devices were shredded. Now we can prove it.” - Sustainability lead, consultancy

docs.x: How a school-supplies manufacturer ships B-grade stock, samples and discontinued lines straight to matched NGOs - tracking number as handover, documentation per match.

docs.t: Does collection have to run through sur.plus?
docs.x: No. Companies that can ship themselves record the tracking number in the dashboard; together with the NGO’s confirmation of receipt that is the handover record. Logistics partners are there for larger lots.

docs.t: What does Tree deliver that Seed does not?
docs.x: Unlimited matches, priority matching, CSRD documentation per match with an audit trail and a donation certificate per match. For recurring weekly lots under a reporting duty, that is the difference between an estimate and evidence.

docs.t: A parcel every week
docs.x: How a school-supplies manufacturer ships B-grade stock, samples and discontinued lines straight from its own warehouse to matched NGOs - the tracking number is the handover, the Tree subscription supplies the documentation. Illustrative example. This scenario shows a typical trigger and the process the platform is built for. Companies and recipients are deliberately unnamed; figures are illustrative and follow the Impact Calculator methodology (GHG Protocol, GIIN IRIS+, tax effect versus disposal). Real cases will replace these examples as soon as pilot partners release them.
docs.p: A Parcel a Week: Direct Shipping to NGOs on Tree

docs.t: The trigger
docs.x: A school-supplies manufacturer with 1,100 employees is subject to reporting. Its surplus is continuous and small: B-grade stock with print defects, samples from sales, discontinued lines after a range change. About 25 kilos a week, manufacturing cost around €600. Too little for a collection, too much for the liquidator, who only takes full pallets. So it sat in the remainder warehouse, 60 square metres, until someone decided. “We sent parcels to schools when someone asked. For the report that was nothing - no value, no recipient, no date.” - Sustainability Manager, school-supplies manufacturer
docs.p: A Parcel a Week: Direct Shipping to NGOs on Tree

docs.t: The process
docs.x: The manufacturer took the Tree subscription. Five users: warehouse, inside sales, sustainability, marketing, accounting. The process was built on what the warehouse already does - pack and ship parcels: Monday: the warehouse lists the week’s surplus as one lot with a contents list. Priority matching against reported needs: school associations, homework clubs, children’s homes, a station mission. docs.t: Returns Direct to a Social Hub: Pilot Design
docs.x: Pilot design: how an e-shop routes low-value returns by label straight to a social logistics partner instead of its warehouse - grading there, evidence per parcel.

docs.t: Why not ship straight to the clothing bank?
docs.x: Because nobody has seen the goods. Ungraded returns turn the NGO into a returns desk, provide no evidence per item and no defensible VAT base. The detour via a grading social partner solves all three.

docs.t: Does this need an integration into the shop system?
docs.x: One additional option in the returns portal and a weekly reconciliation file - nothing more. Because several parties and recurring volumes are involved, the case belongs in an Enterprise offer, not in Seed or Tree.

docs.t: The return that never reaches the warehouse
docs.x: Pilot design for an Enterprise offer: how an e-shop routes low-value items, where the return costs more than the goods are worth, by label straight to a social logistics partner - grading there, evidence per parcel, no detour via the central warehouse. Illustrative example. This scenario shows a typical trigger and the process the platform is built for. Companies and recipients are deliberately unnamed; figures are illustrative and follow the Impact Calculator methodology (GHG Protocol, GIIN IRIS+, tax effect versus disposal). Real cases will replace these examples as soon as pilot partners release them.
docs.p: Returns Direct to a Social Hub: Pilot Design

docs.t: The trigger
docs.x: An e-shop for home textiles and accessories with 1,500 employees has a segment where the return costs more than the goods: items under €25. Return shipping around €4.50, intake and grading around €3, then often outlet or destruction - which for a company this size has required an evidenced donation attempt for textiles since July 2026. Around 9,000 items a year. The obvious idea, sending the return straight to an NGO, fails on three points: nobody has seen the goods, the NGO becomes a returns desk, and there is no evidence per item. That is why this case is a pilot design , not a live case. “Sending returns straight to a clothing bank sounds good until you picture what is in the parcels.” - Head of Returns, e-shop
docs.p: Returns Direct to a Social Hub: Pilot Design

docs.t: The design
docs.x: The rule: only items below the cost threshold, only categories recipients have asked for (bedding, towels, socks, hats). For those the returns portal offers “refund, return to our social partner” - one additional option, no system integration. The recipient is a hub: the label does not lead to a clothing bank but to a social department store with a work-integration programme from the sur.plus network of social service partners. Every parcel is opened and graded there: saleable, limited, unusable. Only then do the goods go to clothing banks and social department stores in the region, unusable items to recycling. The evidence: the grading record per parcel is the proof of the donation attempt and at the same time the basis for the VAT assessment. Weekly reconciliation file between hub, shop and sur.plus. CSRD documentation and donation certificate per lot as in the Tree subscription. What
docs.p: Returns Direct to a Social Hub: Pilot Design

docs.t: The honest maths
docs.x: Whatever arrives at the hub in saleable condition is valued at purchase price - no discount there. With a mix of 30 percent saleable, 50 percent limited and 20 percent unusable, VAT comes to around €11,300 a year, the deduction recovers around €3,400, net about minus €7,900. Plus the hub’s grading fee, around €1.20 per parcel. Against that: around €7.50 per item that return shipping and intake used to cost - about €67,000 for 9,000 items - and a donation record that destruction would have required anyway. The case only pays because the goods never had a value at the central warehouse that justified taking them back. “The difference from the original idea: someone opens the parcels before they end up at a clothing bank.” - Head of Returns, e-shop
docs.p: Returns Direct to a Social Hub: Pilot Design

docs.t: What the pilot has to show
docs.x: 9,000 Items a year below the cost threshold ~€67,000 Return shipping and intake that fall away −€7,900 Net tax effect at the assumed condition mix 7.6 t CO₂ avoided (GHG Protocol) if everything runs as planned < 15% Target: share of unusable items at the hub 90 days Go/no-go: volume, condition mix, effort at the hub Pilot design for an Enterprise offer; this case is not yet running. Prerequisites: a social logistics partner with grading capacity in the region, one additional option in the returns portal, a weekly reconciliation file. docs.t: The trigger
docs.x: A fashion retailer with around 1,200 employees closes three stores at quarter end. The leases require the premises back broom-clean on 31 October. Inside: 120 metres of shelving, 60 clothing rails, 12 fitting rooms, three till counters, mirrors and LED lighting - replacement value around €60,000. Plus 4,200 items of last-season stock, purchase value €48,000, some of it display pieces without tags. The strip-out contractor quoted €5,970 for dismantling and disposing of the fittings. Destroying the stock was not an option: since July 2026 a company of this size must evidence a donation attempt before destroying unsold clothing. “We had two problems with one deadline: get rid of the fittings and hand over the stock cleanly. Until now that meant two contractors and two binders.” - Head of Expansion & Property, fashion retailer
docs.p: Store Closure: Shop Fittings and Stock Donated

docs.t: The process
docs.x: Six weeks before the handover the retailer listed the surplus as a one-off clearance project at a fixed price - three lots of fittings, one per store, and one lot of stock with a condition class. Store managers photographed to the sur.plus template: quantities, dimensions, condition, collection window. No system access, no integration. Fittings: three social department stores in the region - they run retail floors themselves and needed exactly shelving, rails and counters. Collection by the logistics partner inside the strip-out window, two days per store. Stock: two clothing banks with collection capacity. The goods were valued as “limited saleability” - so the VAT on the donation is assessed properly instead of being glossed over. Evidence: the donation offer, recipient responses and handover records sit in the evidence pack - the documentation the destruction ban requires.

docs.t: · Advocacy — In 12+ EU member states, destroying surplus is cheaper than donating it.
docs.x: · Advocacy In 12+ EU member states, destroying surplus is cheaper than donating it. End the VAT penalty on in-kind donations. Donate goods from business assets and you pay VAT as if you had sold them (a “deemed supply”) - destroying them triggers none. Remove that tax and the incentive to destroy usable goods disappears, the red tape ends, and donating becomes cheaper for companies and far easier for aid organisations. docs.t: The story behind sur.plus — From Varanasi to a table in Taiwan.
docs.x: Florian Lechner Founder, sur.plus Read the full story on LinkedIn → 05 The story behind sur.plus From Varanasi to a table in Taiwan. In Varanasi, I volunteered in a classroom that was short of pens, notebooks and school backpacks. 46 days later I sat in a ramen restaurant in Tainan, next to a Chinese leather-goods maker. She told me that returns with minor flaws get scrapped. Surplus bags. The kids I'd bought school supplies for flashed into my head. So I asked her to find donation recipients for those returns. This is no isolated case. Too much gets thrown away too soon - not out of bad will, but because donating takes too much effort. Goodwill was never the problem. Effort is. docs.t: In 12+ EU member states, destroying surplus is cheaper than donating it.
docs.x: End the VAT penalty on in-kind donations. Donate goods from business assets and you pay VAT as if you had sold them (a “deemed supply”) - destroying them triggers none. Remove that tax and the incentive to destroy usable goods disappears, the red tape ends, and donating becomes cheaper for companies and far easier for aid organisations. We’re calling on the EU to fix this at the source. docs.t: Is sur.plus an in-kind donation platform?
docs.x: By category, yes - if you are looking for an in-kind donation platform for companies , this is it. We still call ourselves infrastructure , and the distinction is not word-play. A platform provides a marketplace: supply in, demand in, the parties sort out the rest. That is precisely where in-kind donations fail - not for lack of goodwill, but because of the work in between. Who takes 40 desks, and by when? Is the organisation genuinely charitable? Who coordinates the handover, and how much of it survives an audit? sur.plus does that work: recipient verification, coordinated matching, handover documentation and the evidence that tax and sustainability reporting require. Hence infrastructure - something you rely on, not something you operate.

docs.t: What types of surplus does sur.plus accept - and what is excluded?
docs.x: sur.plus handles non-perishable, usable goods: IT & electronics, office furniture, textiles & clothing, tools & machinery, stationery and retail goods : returns, overstock, end-of-line and seasonal stock from retail and e-commerce. Retailers and online shops can pass on returns that can no longer be sold as donations instead of destroying them. Items must be in usable condition. Deliberately excluded to protect NGOs and people served: Food & beverages (cold-chain and food safety certification required) · Pharmaceuticals & medical devices (regulatory approval required) · Hazardous materials (EU-classified) · Weapons & controlled items (export control). These exclusions are a design choice, not a limitation.

docs.t: FAQ: In-Kind Donations via sur.plus - All Questions and Answers
docs.x: All answers on in-kind donations via sur.plus: process, tax and VAT, CSRD evidence, NGO verification, pricing - with a direct link per question.

docs.t: What types of surplus does sur.plus accept - and what is excluded?
docs.x: sur.plus handles non-perishable, usable goods: IT & electronics, office furniture, textiles & clothing, tools & machinery, stationery and general warehouse overstock. Items must be in usable condition. Deliberately excluded to protect NGOs and people served: Food & beverages (cold-chain and food safety certification required) · Pharmaceuticals & medical devices (regulatory approval required) · Hazardous materials (EU-classified) · Weapons & controlled items (export control). These exclusions are a design choice, not a limitation.

docs.t: Is sur.plus only for large companies?
docs.x: Not at all. A 10-person company with 20 surplus chairs can be exactly the right match for a small local NGO. The Seed plan is built precisely for smaller and purpose-driven businesses. The match doesn’t care about company size; it cares about category, geography and need. Private individuals are welcome too: email service@surpluspurpose.com with a short description of what you have and we’ll personally help you find a verified NGO near you - no account or subscription needed.

docs.t: How does the AI matching work?
docs.x: In the current phase, matching is human-coordinated - Florian and the team personally review listings and make introductions. This ensures quality over speed and lets us build the proprietary transaction data that will train our matching engine. As listing volume grows, AI-assisted matching will activate across compatible categories. Every match, regardless of how it is made, requires confirmation from both sides before anything moves.

docs.t: What about IT hardware - is it complex to donate?
docs.x: IT hardware requires data deletion to GDPR standards before handover. sur.plus provides clear guidelines for each category and the matching process accounts for this. Demand from NGOs for IT equipment is among the highest. We guide you through the process - it’s well-defined and manageable. For larger volumes, certified refurbishment partners handle data wiping, refurbishment and setup documentation - devices arrive ready to use. For smaller handovers, receiving NGOs get a guided Self-Setup Kit. Partners such as Labdoo.org repurpose donated laptops for schools.

docs.t: What does CSRD documentation look like?
docs.x: Every match generates a structured impact report: item description, quantity, receiving organisation, verified delivery confirmation, calculated avoided CO₂ emissions (GHG Protocol), social resource value (GIIN IRIS+) and ESRS-aligned summary metrics. Exportable as PDF and structured data (JSON/CSV).

docs.t: How does sur.plus prevent greenwashing?
docs.x: Every number sur.plus reports is built to be checked. Impact figures are clearly labelled as estimates, calculated with conservative factors under published methodologies (GHG Protocol avoided emissions, GIIN IRIS+ social resource value) - we report avoided emissions from reuse, never offset-based “climate neutral” claims. Every impact report and social media impact card carries its methodology label, date and match ID, so any figure can be traced back to a verified delivery. This matters from September 2026: under the EU Empowering Consumers Directive (2024/825), generic or unsubstantiated green claims become unlawful - sur.plus documentation is designed to give your claims the substantiation they will need.

docs.t: EmpCo from 27 September 2026: what can we still say about our donations?
docs.x: From that date the Empowering Consumers Directive (2024/825) applies, in Germany through the amended UWG. Towards consumers, four kinds of statement become unlawful outright: generic environmental claims without proof (“sustainable”, “climate-friendly”, “green”), climate-neutrality claims based on offsetting, self-made sustainability labels, and vague future promises without a verifiable plan. Alongside that, the general ban on misleading advertising applies to every company, B2B included - competitors and associations can issue warning letters. What remains allowed is what is specific, quantified and substantiated: “120 laptops reused instead of scrapped, five non-profit recipients, avoided emissions calculated under GHG Protocol methodology, dated, outside our own inventory.” That is exactly how every sur.plus figure is built: method label, date and match ID sit on every impact report

docs.t: Does sur.plus issue CO₂ certificates or offsets?
docs.x: No - and we don’t plan to. Avoided emissions from reuse are not offsets. They are reported separately from your GHG inventory, as the GHG Protocol requires, and cannot be netted against your own emissions or sold as credits. Under ESRS E1, carbon credits have to be disclosed separately anyway and do not count towards reduction targets - so a certificate would be of no use to you in your report. What we deliver is what actually counts: method-labelled, verified avoided-emissions data per match for your own Scope 3 disclosure and for claims you can substantiate. We calculate the numbers; we do not earn from their size.

docs.t: What happens when CSRD or ESRS rules change?
docs.x: You don’t have to keep up - that’s our job. sur.plus tracks the moving parts of the regulation - ESRS standards, the Voluntary Standard that replaces VSME for suppliers, the CSRD Omnibus package and VAT rules on in-kind donations - and updates the reporting templates accordingly, supported by ESG Vibe, our in-house ESG-monitoring tool. Documentation you have already generated stays valid; new matches automatically use the current format. Annual ESRS updates are included from Tree.

docs.t: How does support work?
docs.x: Support runs via the live chat on this site - direct, personal and fast. No tickets, no queues. Tree customers get priority response. Prefer email? Reach us at service@surpluspurpose.com - just mention your organisation in the subject line.

docs.t: What is the sur.plus Impact Pledge?
docs.x: The Impact Pledge is an intention, not a fund that already exists - it starts once sur.plus generates revenue. A contribution of 3-5% of net revenues is planned, scaling to 10% depending on quarterly profitability. The pool is meant for emergencies, not routine operations. This structure ensures long-term sustainability of the business while maintaining a strong and credible impact commitment. The three uses of the pool are: (1) NGO Emergency Fund - direct support for NGOs with urgent needs and no matching partner yet; (2) Surplus Rescue Grants - covering transport costs when logistics would otherwise prevent a match; (3) Independent Impact Audit - external academic review of our impact data, so the documentation we hand you rests on more than our own word. The exact quarterly contribution rate and full breakdown are published publicly each quarter.

docs.t: Is sur.plus compliant with the EU AI Act?
docs.x: Yes - sur.plus falls under the minimal to limited risk category of the EU AI Act and is not classified as high-risk AI (Annex III). High-risk systems include AI used in credit scoring, hiring decisions, or critical infrastructure - surplus matching is none of these. As a deployer (not a provider) of general-purpose AI models, sur.plus benefits from significantly lighter obligations than AI model developers. In practice, this means: Transparency (Art. 50) - users are informed when AI is involved in match recommendations No autonomous decisions - all matches are recommendations; humans confirm every donation CSRD documentation - framed as decision-support, not automated assessment Full compliance timeline - AI Act obligations phase in through August 2026; sur.plus is structured to be ready For Enterprise customers requiring formal AI Act documentation, sur.plus can provide a deployer compl

docs.t: Is my data secure - and what happens if I change or cancel my plan?
docs.x: sur.plus is built and operated within the EU. All data is stored and processed within the EU. We comply with GDPR (EU 2016/679), apply data minimisation principles, and never share data with third parties without explicit consent. Plan upgrades take effect immediately; downgrades and cancellations at the end of the current billing period - any time, with no penalty and no lock-in. If you cancel, your data remains accessible for 30 days for export. After that, all personal and company data is permanently deleted on request. We do not sell, rent or use your surplus data for any purpose outside the platform.

docs.t: How does sur.plus handle cross-border shipments and customs outside the EU?
docs.x: sur.plus operates across Europe and beyond - EU member states, the UK, Norway, Switzerland, and as we expand, Global South markets. Cross-border shipments within the EU are straightforward - no customs declarations required for intra-EU transfers. For non-EU countries (UK, Switzerland, Norway, and globally), customs declarations are required on both sides. The principles are similar regardless of country: Non-EU shipments (UK, Switzerland, Norway and beyond): These countries are third countries for EU customs purposes. Shipments require declarations in both directions. Key points: UK imports: UK Global Tariff applies; simplified procedures available for humanitarian shipments under HMRC charitable relief provisions EU imports from UK: EU customs law applies; NGOs with recognised charitable status may qualify for duty relief sur.plus provides all documentation needed for customs filing: i

docs.t: Aren’t there free ways to donate surplus?
docs.x: Yes - free non-profit intermediaries exist, and for a simple handover of new merchandise they are often the right route; we’ll happily say so. What they don’t cover is what a clearance actually requires: logistics, certified data erasure, multi-NGO distribution, and evidence that stands up later. Since the destruction ban that second part matters for unsold stock too - the derogation turns on being able to show who was offered the goods, when , and what they answered . That is the case sur.plus handles - at a published fixed price, with the NGO side free of charge.

docs.t: Is VAT due on an in-kind donation?
docs.x: In Germany, usually yes. Giving away an asset from the business is a deemed supply under sec. 3(1b) UStG, assessed under sec. 10(4) UStG at the notional purchase price at the time of the transfer - not at what you originally paid. For used equipment that figure is often far lower than companies expect. Two common misconceptions are worth clearing up: the zero-rating in the German Federal Ministry of Finance letter of 18 March 2021 only covers goods of limited marketability - unsold but still saleable stock does not qualify - and the pandemic-era relief has expired . We put the figure in the quote before you decide. The mechanics are set out in our German tax guide , and the deduction cap calculator works out how much your company may deduct at all. Other EU member states treat this differently. We are not tax advisers - please confirm your case with your own.

docs.t: How is the €2,250 scrapping comparison calculated?
docs.x: From three items that typically arise in an IT refresh of around 180 devices: certified data erasure at roughly €780 , container and disposal at roughly €300 , and about 18 hours of internal handling, costed at roughly €1,170 - coordination, sign-off, documentation. That last item never appears in a disposal contractor’s quote and gets paid all the same. The figure varies with volume, device type and region; treat it as an orientation value, not a price list. Your actual comparison goes in the quote.

docs.t: What exactly does sur.plus take on under the destruction ban?
docs.x: Since July 2026 larger companies may no longer destroy unsold textiles, clothing accessories and footwear. One of the exemptions covers stock that was demonstrably donated or offered for donation - and that attempt has to be documented: the offer to at least three social economy entities in the EU or an equivalent public offer, a window of at least eight weeks, and every response logged, including the refusals. That is the process the Clearance project runs for you, handing over the evidence. Background and deadlines are in our guide to the EU destruction ban .

docs.t: Wouldn’t selling used IT to a refurbisher be the better deal?
docs.x: Sometimes, yes. If your fleet is young and valuable, selling to an IT refurbisher can make more financial sense - and if that’s your situation, we’ll tell you so in the quote. Clearance is built for the mixed reality of a move, refresh or closure: aging devices, furniture and equipment where residual value is low but social value and reporting value are high - and where you want donation certificates and audit-ready documentation instead of a buyback note.

docs.t: EmpCo from 27 September 2026: what can we still say about our donations?
docs.x: From that date the Empowering Consumers Directive (2024/825) applies, in Germany through the amended UWG. Towards consumers, four kinds of statement become unlawful outright: generic environmental claims without proof (“sustainable”, “climate-friendly”, “green”), climate-neutrality claims based on offsetting, self-made sustainability labels, and vague future promises without a verifiable plan. Alongside that, the general ban on misleading advertising applies to every company, B2B included - competitors and associations can issue warning letters. What remains allowed is what is specific, quantified and substantiated: “120 laptops reused instead of scrapped, five non-profit recipients, avoided emissions calculated under GHG Protocol methodology, dated, outside our own inventory.” That is exactly how every sur.plus figure is built: method label, date and match ID sit on every impact report

docs.t: What data we collect and why
docs.x: This website collects no personal data for analytics purposes. No cookies are set and no tracking pixels are used. The following may occur through your use of the site: Server logs - your IP address and browser type may be stored temporarily by our hosting provider (Netlify) for security and operation. Legal basis: legitimate interest (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR). Retention: usually up to 30 days by the provider. See Netlify’s Privacy Policy . Live chat - if you write to us in the chat, your messages (and the email address you may optionally add for replies) are stored in our EU-hosted database (processor: Supabase, EU region) so we can answer you. A random conversation ID stays in your browser's local storage so you can see replies on this device - not a tracking cookie, no personal identification. Legal basis: to respond to your request (Art. 6(1)(b)/(f) GDPR). Retention: deleted on request; ot

docs.t: EU Circular Economy
docs.x: Since 19 July 2026 the EU Ecodesign Regulation prohibits large companies from destroying unsold clothing, clothing accessories, headgear and footwear. Destruction because nobody took the goods is only defensible if you can evidence that they were offered - to at least three social economy entities in the EU, or on your own website - for at least eight weeks. Medium-sized companies follow on 19 July 2030. Separately, Article 24 makes large companies publish annually what unsold consumer goods they discarded, across all product categories. From 27 September 2026

docs.x: sur.plus handles non-perishable, usable goods: IT & electronics, office furniture, textiles & clothing, tools & machinery, stationery and retail goods : returns, overstock, end-of-line and seasonal stock from retail and e-commerce. Retailers and online shops can pass on returns that can no longer be sold as donations instead of destroying them. Items must be in usable condition. Deliberately excluded to protect NGOs and people served: Food & beverages (cold-chain and food safety certification required) · Pharmaceuticals & medical devices (regulatory approval required) · Hazardous materials (EU-classified) · Weapons & controlled items (export control). These exclusions are a design choice, not a limitation.
docs.p: For Companies: Donate Surplus Instead of Disposal

docs.t: Is sur.plus only for large companies?
docs.x: Not at all. A 10-person company with 20 surplus chairs can be exactly the right match for a small local NGO. The Seed plan is built precisely for smaller and purpose-driven businesses. The match doesn’t care about company size; it cares about category, geography and need. Private individuals are welcome too: email service@surpluspurpose.com with a short description of what you have and we’ll personally help you find a verified NGO near you - no account or subscription needed.
docs.p: For Companies: Donate Surplus Instead of Disposal

docs.t: What about IT hardware - is it complex to donate?
docs.x: IT hardware requires data deletion to GDPR standards before handover. sur.plus provides clear guidelines for each category and the matching process accounts for this. Demand from NGOs for IT equipment is among the highest. We guide you through the process - it’s well-defined and manageable. For larger volumes, certified refurbishment partners handle data wiping, refurbishment and setup documentation - devices arrive ready to use. For smaller handovers, receiving NGOs get a guided Self-Setup Kit. Partners such as Labdoo.org repurpose donated laptops for schools. Read more in the guide: Donating corporate IT (GDPR) →
docs.p: For Companies: Donate Surplus Instead of Disposal

docs.t: What does CSRD documentation look like?
docs.x: Every match generates a structured impact report: item description, quantity, receiving organisation, verified delivery confirmation, calculated avoided CO₂ emissions ( GHG Protocol ), social resource value ( GIIN IRIS+ ) and ESRS-aligned summary metrics. Exportable as PDF and structured data (JSON/CSV). Read more in the guide: In-kind donations in ESRS E5 →
docs.p: For Companies: Donate Surplus Instead of Disposal

docs.t: How does sur.plus prevent greenwashing?
docs.x: Every number sur.plus reports is built to be checked. Impact figures are clearly labelled as estimates, calculated with conservative factors under published methodologies ( GHG Protocol avoided emissions, GIIN IRIS+ social resource value) - we report avoided emissions from reuse, never offset-based “climate neutral” claims. Every impact report and social media impact card carries its methodology label, date and match ID, so any figure can be traced back to a verified delivery. This matters from September 2026: under the EU Empowering Consumers Directive (2024/825), generic or unsubstantiated green claims become unlawful - sur.plus documentation is designed to give your claims the substantiation they will need.
docs.p: For Companies: Donate Surplus Instead of Disposal

docs.t: EmpCo from 27 September 2026: what can we still say about our donations?
docs.x: From that date the Empowering Consumers Directive (2024/825) applies, in Germany through the amended UWG. Towards consumers, four kinds of statement become unlawful outright: generic environmental claims without proof (“sustainable”, “climate-friendly”, “green”), climate-neutrality claims based on offsetting, self-made sustainability labels, and vague future promises without a verifiable plan. Alongside that, the general ban on misleading advertising applies to every company, B2B included - competitors and associations can issue warning letters. What remains allowed is what is specific, quantified and substantiated: “120 laptops reused instead of scrapped, five non-profit recipients, avoided emissions calculated under GHG Protocol methodology, dated, outside our own inventory.” That is exactly how every sur.plus figure is built: method label, date and match ID sit on every impact report
docs.p: For Companies: Donate Surplus Instead of Disposal

docs.t: Does sur.plus issue CO₂ certificates or offsets?
docs.x: No - and we don’t plan to. Avoided emissions from reuse are not offsets. They are reported separately from your GHG inventory, as the GHG Protocol requires, and cannot be netted against your own emissions or sold as credits. Under ESRS E1, carbon credits have to be disclosed separately anyway and do not count towards reduction targets - so a certificate would be of no use to you in your report. What we deliver is what actually counts: method-labelled, verified avoided-emissions data per match for your own Scope 3 disclosure and for claims you can substantiate. We calculate the numbers; we do not earn from their size.
docs.p: For Companies: Donate Surplus Instead of Disposal

docs.t: What counts as one pickup - and when does it become a Clearance project?
docs.x: A First Donation Run covers one pickup : up to two pallets from one collection address on one agreed date, in one category family - IT, or furniture, or tools. In a typical IT mix, two pallets hold around 100 devices. How many NGOs receive the goods is never a limit and never a surcharge - the goods go to as many verified organisations as they need. More than two pallets, several sites or mixed categories make it a Clearance & Logistics project: we quote a fixed price before we start, and if you booked a First Donation Run within the last 12 months, its full price is credited.
docs.p: For Companies: Donate Surplus Instead of Disposal

docs.t: How does platform access work?
docs.x: Three steps. Pulse is the 10-minute assessment - no account, your impact potential as a PDF. Registration is free and opens the platform: browse what verified NGOs need right now - anonymised, with category, focus and region. Seed or Tree unlock the part that costs us work: who is behind a need, direct contact, a human-coordinated match, and the donation certificate that comes with it - plus, on Tree, the CSRD documentation per match. All connections stay on-platform, ToS-enforced. All questions & answers Part of Germany’s impact ecosystem CIRCULAR REPUBLIC 07 Ready to start?

docs.t: Donating corporate IT under the GDPR: reuse instead of shredding
docs.x: The GDPR requires a state, not physical destruction. Why ISO/IEC 21964 replaced DIN 66399, what a defensible IT donation process must evidence per device, and why only about 1.9 per cent of treated e-waste is prepared for reuse.

docs.t: Does the GDPR require physical destruction of storage media?
docs.x: No. Through storage limitation in Article 5 and the right to erasure in Article 17, the GDPR requires a state (the data must no longer be available) and through the accountability principle in Article 5(2) the ability to demonstrate it. Physical destruction is one possible route, not a prescribed one.

docs.t: Is DIN 66399 still current?
docs.x: The standard has been withdrawn. Its content was transferred in 2018 into the international standard ISO/IEC 21964. Contracts and process documents should reference that.

docs.t: How much electronic equipment is actually reused?
docs.x: According to provisional figures from the German Federal Statistical Office, of around 920,000 tonnes of waste electrical and electronic equipment treated in 2024, 17,600 tonnes were prepared for reuse, about 1.9 per cent, and 6.3 per cent less than in 2023. Around 758,000 tonnes were recycled. The reported 84.3 per cent recycling rate covers recycling and preparation for reuse together.

docs.t: Does an IT donation need an erasure certificate?
docs.x: There is no legally prescribed form for an erasure certificate; such documents are market practice. What matters legally is the ability to demonstrate effective erasure under the GDPR accountability principle. Evidence per device (serial number, method, date, result) is therefore more useful than a collective protocol.

docs.t: Is a refurbisher receiving storage media a processor under Article 28 GDPR?
docs.x: That depends on the specific arrangement, in particular whether and when the provider has access to personal data still present. The classification and any Article 28 agreement should be settled before the first handover.

docs.t: Contents
docs.x: The number that describes the problem Why the shredder wins Standards: what DIN 66399 means today What a defensible IT donation process must do The side effect: two records from one transaction When corporate IT is retired, the shredder almost always wins. Not because it is the better option, but because it answers the question "what about the data?" most unambiguously. This guide shows how that answer can be just as unambiguous without destroying the device.
docs.p: Donating corporate IT under the GDPR: reuse instead of shredding

docs.t: The number that describes the problem
docs.x: EU-wide reuse statistics for electronic equipment are patchy. Germany publishes among the most detailed, and the pattern it reveals is not specifically German. 920,000 t waste electrical and electronic equipment treated Germany, 2024, provisional 758,000 t recycled (+1.5 % on 2023) Germany, 2024, provisional 17,600 t prepared for reuse (−6.3 % on 2023) Germany, 2024, provisional 17,600 of 920,000 tonnes is about 1.9 per cent . Over 98 per cent goes to recycling, other recovery or disposal, even though the waste hierarchy in Article 4(1) of Directive 2008/98/EC places preparing for re-use above recycling. And the reuse figure fell by 6.3 per cent while recycling rose. For a three-year-old notebook from a hardware refresh, that is not a technical necessity. It is a process decision nobody explicitly takes. A reading note on that statistic: the reported recycling rate of 84.3 per cent cover
docs.p: Donating corporate IT under the GDPR: reuse instead of shredding

docs.t: Why the shredder wins
docs.x: The internal reasoning runs the same way almost everywhere: the devices held personal data; the GDPR requires erasure; certified destruction produces a certificate; therefore destroy. The short circuit is in the third step. The GDPR requires that data not be kept longer than necessary (storage limitation, Article 5) and that data subjects can obtain erasure (Article 17). It does not require that the storage medium be physically destroyed. What is required is a state (the data is no longer recoverable) and, through the accountability principle in Article 5(2), the ability to demonstrate that state. Physical destruction is one route there. An effective, documented erasure procedure is another. The difference: the first ends the device's useful life, the second does not.
docs.p: Donating corporate IT under the GDPR: reuse instead of shredding

docs.t: Standards: what DIN 66399 means today
docs.x: Tenders and quotes across the German-speaking market still reference "DIN 66399". The standard governed data carrier destruction in three parts, defined three protection classes and material-specific security levels: H1 to H7 for magnetic media, for example. Important for your documents: DIN 66399 has been withdrawn. Its content was transferred in 2018 into the international standard ISO/IEC 21964 . Contracts, process descriptions and certificates should reference ISO/IEC 21964 today. Equally important is what these standards do not cover: they specify requirements for destruction . For the case "the device survives, the data must go" they are not the applicable reference, and that case is barely documented anywhere. The entire professional conversation on the topic is about destruction.
docs.p: Donating corporate IT under the GDPR: reuse instead of shredding

docs.t: What a defensible IT donation process must do
docs.x: Separate device classes Not every device is suitable. Systems with special licences, embedded security modules or production-critical firmware do not belong in the same process as standard notebooks from a refresh. Fix the erasure method before the first device Which procedure, which software, which evidence per serial number? The method must match the medium type; solid-state drives behave differently from classic hard disks. Evidence per device, not per batch Serial number, date, method, result, performing party. A collective protocol without device-level detail is worthless when questioned. Settle roles before anything leaves the building Who erases — you or a service provider? Where a provider has access to media before erasure, the data protection role of that provider needs to be settled contractually. This belongs before the first transport, not after. Verify the recipient Charita
docs.p: Donating corporate IT under the GDPR: reuse instead of shredding

docs.t: The side effect: two records from one transaction
docs.x: A properly documented IT donation process produces evidence you need in two other places. For tax purposes: valuation, handover record and donation confirmation — see the guide to VAT and tax on in-kind donations . For sustainability reporting: weight and destination, which is exactly what ESRS E5 asks for. Shred the devices and you have a disposal invoice. Pass them on and you have a record that fits three systems. A note on our own product
docs.p: Donating corporate IT under the GDPR: reuse instead of shredding

docs.t: What sur.plus does with IT donations — and what stays with you
docs.x: sur.plus matches devices to verified charitable recipients and consolidates handover and destination records in one file per transaction, including your per-serial erasure evidence, where you supply it. sur.plus does not perform the data erasure. That stays with your IT team or a certified partner, and the data protection assessment of the process belongs to your data protection officer. Providers promising "donation including data protection from a single source, no assessment needed" are promising too much. You will not get that promise from us.

docs.t: EU destruction ban 2026: what companies must document
docs.x: Since 19 July 2026 the ESPR destruction ban applies to large companies EU-wide. The ten derogations, why an evidenced donation offer to at least three EU social economy entities over eight weeks matters, and what must be kept for five years.

docs.t: When does the EU destruction ban apply?
docs.x: For large companies since 19 July 2026, for medium-sized companies from 19 July 2030. Small and micro companies are exempt. The SME definition in Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC applies: a company is an SME if it employs fewer than 250 persons and has either turnover of at most 50 million euro or a balance sheet total of at most 43 million euro.

docs.t: Which products are covered?
docs.x: Currently clothing including headgear, clothing accessories and footwear, defined via Combined Nomenclature codes in Annex VII of the Ecodesign Regulation. Further product groups can be added by delegated act.

docs.t: Must goods be donated before they may be destroyed?
docs.x: There is no obligation to donate. Article 2(h) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296 lists an unsuccessful donation offer as a derogation. The product must have been offered either directly to at least three suitable social economy entities located within the Union, or on an easily accessible page of the operator's own website, for a period of at least eight weeks, and not have been accepted. The ground is subsidiary: it applies only where none of points (a) to (g) is applicable.

docs.t: How many organisations must be approached?
docs.x: For the direct route, at least three suitable social economy entities located within the Union. Alternatively, an offer on an easily accessible page of the economic operator's website is sufficient. Either way the offer must run for at least eight weeks.

docs.t: How long must destruction records be kept?
docs.x: Under Article 3(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296, five years after the product concerned has been destroyed. On request by the competent authority they must be made available in electronic form within 30 days of receipt of the request.

docs.t: What does the Article 24 disclosure obligation add?
docs.x: Disclosure of the number and weight of destroyed products, the reasons for destruction and the waste treatment operations applied, no later than twelve months after the end of the financial year. It covers consumer products generally, not only the Annex VII scope. The detailed format under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2 applies to financial years beginning on or after 2 March 2027.

docs.t: Do donated products count as destroyed?
docs.x: No. Under the recitals of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2 donated products are not treated as discarded, because the intention to discard is absent.

docs.t: The EU destruction ban from 19 July 2026: what companies must document now
docs.x: The Ecodesign Regulation's destruction ban is in force across the EU. The real effort lies not in the prohibition but in the evidence duty, and in one derogation that turns a documented donation offer into a precondition. Updated: 7 August 2026 Legal status: August 2026 Reading time: 10 min
docs.p: EU destruction ban 2026: what companies must document

docs.t: Contents
docs.x: What applies since 19 July 2026 The exemptions, and why one of them touches your process The documentation duty is where the effort sits National implementation: the German example Why this interlocks with reporting Since 19 July 2026, large companies may no longer simply destroy unsold clothing, headgear, clothing accessories and footwear in the EU. That is the obvious part. The part that changes processes sits in the exemptions: a company that wants to destroy must be able to evidence the ground it relies on: for five years, producible within 30 days. And one of those grounds is an unsuccessful offer to donate . For the first time, in-kind donation stops being a sustainability nice-to-have and becomes a documented compliance step . Donation itself is not mandated: what is required is evidence that the goods were genuinely offered before being destroyed.

docs.x: The legal basis is the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 (ESPR). The prohibition itself sits in Article 25(1) , the disclosure obligation in Article 24 ; Annex VII defines the product scope. Company size Destruction ban applies from Large companies 19 July 2026 Medium-sized companies 19 July 2030 Small and micro companies exempt The size threshold is widely misquoted. The ESPR refers to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC. Under it, a company is an SME if it employs fewer than 250 persons and has either an annual turnover of at most €50m or a balance sheet total of at most €43m. Read the other way round, "large company" means 250 or more employees — or , below 250 employees, turnover above €50m and a balance sheet total above €43m, cumulatively. A company with 120 employees, €80m turnover and a €30m balance sheet total remains medium-sized : bound from 2030,

docs.x: Destruction remains permissible where a recognised ground applies. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296 of 9 February 2026 sets out those derogations: it does not define the prohibition, it defines the exceptions to it. Its Article 2 lists ten grounds, (a) to (j): the product is dangerous within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2023/988 non-compliance with Union or national law, where destruction is required or is an appropriate corrective measure infringement of intellectual property rights expiry of a licence or contractual term for IP-protected products trade marks, logos or design features cannot technically be removed damage, deterioration or contamination where repair or refurbishment is not technically or economically feasible design or manufacturing defects where repair is not technically feasible an unsuccessful offer to donate (see below) the product was received as a donation by a

docs.t: Ground (h) in its own words
docs.x: Point (h) is subsidiary : it applies expressly only where none of the circumstances in points (a) to (g) is applicable. A company with damaged or legally unsaleable stock does not need it. For usable residual stock it is the only workable route, and it requires three things at once: The product was offered for donation — either directly to at least three suitable social economy entities located within the Union , or on an easily accessible page of the economic operator's own website . The offer ran for at least eight weeks . The period applies to both routes. The product was not accepted for donation . The operational consequence: a company relying on this ground must be able to show who was approached (at least three, EU-based), when the period started, how the offer was documented, and that it was not accepted. An informal note saying "we tried" is not evidence in front of a market sur

docs.t: The documentation duty is where the effort sits
docs.x: 5 years retention, running from the destruction of each product 30 days to produce records in electronic form on request 8 weeks minimum duration of an evidenced donation offer Under Article 3(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296 , records must be kept for five years after the product concerned has been destroyed and made available to the competent authorities in electronic form within 30 days of receipt of the request . Article 4 in addition requires a declaration of the applicable derogation to the waste operator. This is a hold-and-produce duty, not a notification duty, the effort arises in your warehouse, your logistics and your filing, not at the authority. And the clock runs per product from its destruction, not from financial year end.

docs.t: Separately: the disclosure obligation under Article 24
docs.x: Distinct from the destruction ban, a considerably broader disclosure obligation applies under Article 24 ESPR . It covers consumer products generally, not only the Annex VII scope: food, feed, medicinal products and vehicles are among the exclusions. Micro and small companies are out of scope; medium-sized companies are covered from 19 July 2030. Companies must disclose the number and weight of destroyed products, the reasons for destruction and the waste treatment operations applied, no later than twelve months after the end of the financial year. The detailed format is set by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2 , which applies to financial years beginning on or after 2 March 2027 . docs.t: National implementation: the German example
docs.x: The ESPR applies directly in every Member State, but enforcement and penalties are national. Germany illustrates the pattern. Its ecodesign modernisation act was signed on 22 June 2026 and published in the Federal Law Gazette on 26 June 2026 (BGBl. 2026 I No. 191). Section 19(3) of the resulting Ecodesign Act provides for administrative fines of up to €100,000 for destruction contrary to Article 25 ESPR and up to €10,000 for breaches of the Article 24 disclosure duties. The act enters into force on 1 November 2026 . Two things follow for any multi-country operation. First, the substantive prohibition has applied since 19 July 2026 regardless of when national sanctions kick in. Second, penalty levels, competent authorities and procedural rules differ by Member State: check them where you actually hold stock, not only where you are headquartered.

docs.t: VAT and tax on corporate in-kind donations in the EU
docs.x: Articles 16 and 74 of the VAT Directive explained: why a gift can be a taxable supply, why the valuation date matters more than the purchase price, what is a member state option, and where cross-border donations stand after Persche and Stauffer.

docs.t: Is VAT due when a company donates goods in the EU?
docs.x: Potentially. Under Article 16 of the VAT Directive 2006/112/EC, disposal of business goods free of charge is treated as a supply for consideration where the VAT on those goods was wholly or partly deductible. If no input VAT was deducted on acquisition, Article 16 does not apply.

docs.t: How is the taxable amount calculated?
docs.x: Under Article 74 of the VAT Directive it is the purchase price of the goods or of similar goods, or in the absence of a purchase price the cost price, determined at the time when the application, disposal or retention takes place. The valuation date is the donation date, not the acquisition date.

docs.t: Can the taxable amount be reduced to zero?
docs.x: At EU level this is addressed only for food, and only in non-binding instruments: a VAT Committee guideline and the Commission's 2017 food donation guidelines, which say the amount should be adjusted to the state of the goods and could even be zero where the food genuinely has no value. We found no equivalent EU-level guidance for non-food goods. In practice a reduced valuation must be reasoned and documented under national rules.

docs.t: Is there an EU VAT exemption for donations to charities?
docs.x: No. Annex III point 1 allows member states to apply a reduced or zero rate to foodstuffs, which is a product category rather than a recipient status. Annex III point 15 and Article 132(1)(g) concern supplies by welfare organisations, not supplies to them. There is no harmonised charity exemption for corporate donors.

docs.t: Is there an EU-wide de-minimis threshold for small gifts?
docs.x: No. Article 16 excludes samples and gifts of small value from the deemed supply rule, but the VAT Directive sets no figure. Each member state defines its own threshold.

docs.t: Is the tax deductibility of in-kind donations harmonised in the EU?
docs.x: No. Deduction caps, valuation rules and recognised purposes are set nationally. EU law constrains national rules through the fundamental freedoms: in Case C-318/07 Persche the Court held that gifts to bodies recognised as charitable in another member state fall under free movement of capital, expressly including gifts made in kind in the form of everyday consumer goods.

docs.t: Is there an EU register of charitable organisations?
docs.x: No. There is no EU-level register, no EU charity status and no mutual recognition of charitable status for tax purposes. Each tax authority applies a comparability test against its own national criteria, and the evidential burden sits with the donor.

docs.t: Are imported donated goods free of customs duty?
docs.x: Council Regulation (EC) No 1186/2009, Articles 61 to 65, grants relief for basic necessities imported by approved charitable or philanthropic organisations for free distribution to those in need, and for equipment and office materials sent free of charge for their operating needs. Alcohol, tobacco, coffee, tea and motor vehicles other than ambulances are excluded. Import VAT is governed separately by Council Directive 2009/132/EC, Article 43.

The VAT treatment is harmonised in principle. The amount is not, and the difference usually sits in a single phrase: when the goods are valued. Harmonised EU-wide: that a gift of business goods can be a taxable supply, and how the taxable amount is calculated. docs.t: Why a free gift can still be a taxable supply
docs.x: Under Article 16 of the VAT Directive 2006/112/EC , the disposal free of charge of goods forming part of a business's assets "shall be treated as a supply of goods for consideration, where the VAT on those goods or the component parts thereof was wholly or partly deductible ". Two consequences follow immediately, and both are often missed: If no input VAT was deducted on acquisition, Article 16 does not apply at all. There is nothing to account for. Article 16 exists precisely to catch gratuitous transfers. A donation is not "outside the scope of VAT" merely because nothing is charged for it. The same article carves out an exception: "the application of goods for business use as samples or as gifts of small value shall not be treated as a supply of goods for consideration". The Directive sets no figure for what "small value" means: each member state defines its own threshold. Any guide q

docs.t: The valuation date is the whole argument
docs.x: Article 74 sets the taxable amount for such a deemed supply as "the purchase price of the goods or of similar goods or, in the absence of a purchase price, the cost price, determined at the time when the application, disposal or retention takes place ". That final clause is the point. The taxable amount is not what you paid for the goods. It is what comparable goods, in their present condition , would cost at the moment you donate them. For six-year-old office chairs, fully depreciated laptops or previous-season stock, that figure is a fraction of the original price, sometimes close to nothing. The finance objection is usually built on the acquisition cost, which is the wrong number.

docs.t: How far down can it go?
docs.x: Here precision matters, because the honest answer is narrower than the one usually given. At EU level there is an agreed position, but only for food , and only in a non-binding instrument. The VAT Committee unanimously agreed, as quoted in the Commission's 2017 EU guidelines on food donation, that where such a donation is treated as a supply for consideration, "the taxable amount shall be the purchase price of the goods … adjusted to the state of those goods at the time when the donation takes place , as provided for in Article 74". The Commission adds that where goods are close to their date marking or unfit for sale but safe, these circumstances "should be taken into account by Member States when determining the VAT due, which could even be zero in cases where the food genuinely has no value". docs.t: And the charity exemption everyone assumes exists?
docs.x: It does not. There is no EU VAT exemption or zero rate for donating goods to a charity . The provisions people reach for do something else: Annex III point (1) allows member states to apply a reduced or zero rate to foodstuffs , a product category, not a recipient status. Where a state uses it, food donations carry that rate anyway. Annex III point (15) and Article 132(1)(g) concern supplies by welfare organisations, not supplies to them. They do not help a corporate donor. So the only routes to zero or near-zero VAT on a corporate in-kind donation are: the member-state "small gift" threshold, a member-state-accepted Article 74 valuation reflecting the goods' actual condition, or (for food only) a national zero rate. All three are national; none is an EU-wide charity relief.

docs.t: There is no EU register of charitable recipients
docs.x: This is worth stating plainly, because it is the most common wrong assumption in cross-border donation planning. No EU-level register, no EU charity status, no mutual recognition for tax purposes. Germany's donation recipient register is a purely national instrument; there is no EU counterpart. The proposed directive on European cross-border associations would create a legal form , not a tax-status register, and it has not been adopted. In practice each tax authority runs a comparability test against its own national public-benefit criteria, and you supply the evidence. docs.t: Importing donated goods from outside the EU
docs.x: Two separate reliefs apply, and they are frequently conflated: Customs duty: Council Regulation (EC) No 1186/2009, Articles 61 to 65, grants relief for basic necessities imported by approved charitable or philanthropic organisations for free distribution to those in need, and for equipment and office materials sent free of charge to such organisations for their own operating needs. Alcohol, tobacco, coffee, tea and motor vehicles other than ambulances are excluded. Approval of the organisation is a national act. Import VAT: a separate instrument (Council Directive 2009/132/EC, Article 43) with the same three categories but a stricter condition for basic necessities, which must be obtained free of charge by the importing organisation. Customs relief does not carry import VAT relief automatically. Check both.

docs.x: On 9 September 2026 the Commission opened the initiative “VAT and the circular economy” (call for evidence for an impact assessment, Ares(2026)8589104, plus a public consultation). Feedback is open until 4 November 2026 ; a proposal for a directive is planned for the second quarter of 2027. The Commission states the problem this guide describes in its own words: the right to deduct input VAT currently makes destroying viable goods more attractive than donating them. docs.t: Green claims on donations: the EmpCo rules
docs.x: From 27 September 2026 the EmpCo rules apply EU-wide. What you may no longer say about in-kind donations, what stays permissible, and the evidence it takes.

docs.t: Does EmpCo apply to us if we only sell to business customers?
docs.x: Partly, and the part that does not apply is smaller than it looks. The blacklist in Annex I of Directive 2005/29/EC covers business-to-consumer practices, but a website, a LinkedIn post or a press release reaches consumers whatever your customers are: what counts is the audience of the statement, not the business model. Independently of that, the general prohibition on misleading actions applies to commercial practices between businesses in several member states, and the leading German case on climate-neutral advertising concerned an advertisement in a food trade journal.

docs.t: Is saying we donate instead of discarding already an environmental claim?
docs.x: Describing the transaction is not: 120 laptops handed over to five non-profit organisations is a statement of fact, evidenced by a handover record. Asserting an effect is: rescued from disposal implies an environmental benefit and needs evidence that the goods would otherwise have been discarded and are being reused by the recipient. Evaluating is the third step and the riskiest: our sustainable donation programme is a generic environmental claim under Annex I point 4a.

docs.t: May we advertise avoided CO2 emissions from a donation?
docs.x: Yes, with method and boundary disclosed, and reported as avoided emissions outside your own inventory as the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard treats them. What is banned from 27 September 2026 is the offsetting-based claim: stating that a product or the company has a neutral, reduced or positive climate impact because emissions were offset (Annex I point 4c). Never net avoided emissions against your own footprint.

docs.t: Our member state has not transposed EmpCo yet. Do we have more time?
docs.x: No, for three reasons. The directive itself sets 27 September 2026 as the date the national provisions apply. docs.t: Is saying we donate already an environmental claim?
docs.x: Not every statement about a donation is. The line runs between describing a transaction and asserting an effect. Transaction: “We handed over 120 laptops to five non-profit organisations.” A statement of fact, evidenced by a handover record. Not an environmental claim. Effect: “We rescued 120 laptops from disposal.” This implies an environmental benefit. The definition now bites, and the sentence needs evidence that the devices would otherwise have been discarded and that the recipient keeps them in use. Evaluation: “Our sustainable donation practice” or “donating green”. A generic environmental claim under point 4a, unlawful without recognised excellent environmental performance. docs.t: What stays permissible: specific, quantified, evidenced
docs.x: The directive does not prohibit talking about environmental effects. It prohibits doing so without evidence. A claim stays permissible when it meets three conditions. Specific: it names what it is about. Not the environment, but the reuse of 120 laptops. Quantified and bounded: it gives a figure and its scope. Not “we save resources”, but “in 2026, 3.8 tonnes of office equipment went to verified non-profit organisations instead of disposal”. Evidenced: the record behind it exists before the sentence is published, and it survives a request to see it. Two safe harbours are worth naming, because they cover most of what companies actually want to say. A factual description of the transaction is not an environmental claim at all. docs.t: The per-transaction evidence, before the claim goes out
docs.x: The order matters. Evidence is assembled before publication, not after a complaint. For a donation, six items carry almost every defensible claim: Category and quantity, by count and by weight. Recipient and date, with a handover confirmation from the receiving organisation. The counterfactual: what would have happened to the goods otherwise, and on what basis you say so. Condition and expected continued use at the recipient, which is what separates reuse from disposal by another route. For any emissions figure: method, emission factors, system boundary, and the label avoided emissions outside the inventory. Who approved the wording, and on which version of the record. None of this is new work if the donation is documented as it happens. It is expensive work if it has to be reconstructed a year later from invoices.
