docs.t: In-kind donations and ESRS E5: what the revised standard requires
docs.x: The revised ESRS E5 has five disclosures — E5-6 was deleted. What E5-4 and E5-5 now require on resource flows and waste, why donated goods are waste prevention rather than preparing for re-use, and the CSRD position after Omnibus I.

docs.t: Which ESRS E5 disclosures cover reuse and waste?
docs.x: In the revised version primarily E5-5 (resource outflows: total weight of waste generated, broken down by recovery and disposal operations including reuse, plus the proportion whose final destination is unknown) and E5-4 (resource inflows: secondary resources used, in weight or as a percentage of the total weight of key materials). E5-1 to E5-3 add narrative disclosures on policies, actions and targets.

docs.t: Does ESRS E5-6 still exist?
docs.x: No. The disclosure on anticipated financial effects was deleted outright in the revised version adopted on 3 July 2026. ESRS E5 now has five disclosures, E5-1 to E5-5.

docs.t: Do the revised ESRS already apply?
docs.x: No. They were adopted as a delegated act on 3 July 2026 but at the time of writing were neither published in the Official Journal nor in force; the Commission itself flags them as not in force. The scrutiny period for Parliament and Council is two months, extendable by two more. The act provides for application to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027.

docs.t: Do the ESRS require in-kind donations to be reported?
docs.x: Not expressly. The words donation or in-kind donation do not appear in the ESRS E5 text, and EFRAG has published no implementation guidance on E5. Passing on usable goods instead of discarding them is however a waste prevention measure and can be presented under E5-2; it affects the resource outflow breakdown in E5-5. That is a derivation, not an express requirement.

docs.t: Is donating goods waste prevention or preparing for re-use?
docs.x: Waste prevention. Under Article 3(16) of Waste Framework Directive 2008/98/EC, preparing for re-use covers only products that have already become waste. A usable item that is passed on is not waste under Article 3(1), because the intention to discard is absent; it falls under re-use in Article 3(13) and therefore under tier (a) of the hierarchy in Article 4(1).

docs.t: Who is still in scope of the CSRD after Omnibus I?
docs.x: Under Directive (EU) 2026/470, undertakings with more than 1,000 employees on average and more than 450 million euro net turnover. Both criteria must be met. For third-country undertakings the thresholds are more than 450 million euro net turnover in the EU plus an EU subsidiary or branch with more than 200 million euro net turnover.

docs.t: What is the value chain cap?
docs.x: The new Article 29ca of Accounting Directive 2013/34/EU prohibits reporting undertakings from requiring more information than the voluntary standard provides from undertakings with at most 1,000 employees. It protects every undertaking up to that size, not only formal SMEs, and does not prevent voluntary disclosure.

docs.t: Where do in-kind donations sit in the Voluntary Standard?
docs.x: In the basic module, disclosure B7 Resource use, circular economy and waste management: application of circular economy principles, total weight of waste generated, and the proportion of waste diverted to recycling or reuse.

docs.t: IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle the old fleet
docs.x: At a hardware refresh the rollout plan decides what happens to the old devices. When selling pays more, what donating means for VAT, and which route leaves which record.

docs.t: Is it better for tax to donate old IT or to sell it?
docs.x: It depends on book value and market value. A sale produces taxable proceeds but brings cash. A donation brings no cash, and in most regimes the tax benefit is tied to a value that is small for depreciated devices. The argument for donating is the documented recipient and re-use, not tax.

docs.t: Is VAT due when we donate used IT?
docs.x: Usually yes, where input VAT was deducted: Art. 16 of the VAT Directive treats disposal free of charge as a supply for consideration, and Art. 74 sets the taxable amount at the purchase price of similar goods at the time of the donation, i.e. the second-hand value. Several Member States have specific relief for donations to charities.

docs.t: Is a working old device waste?
docs.x: Not automatically. Waste is what the holder discards or intends or is required to discard (Art. 3(1) Directive 2008/98/EC). A device that is sold or donated for continued use goes to re-use of a product that is not waste (Art. 3(13)). It becomes WEEE only when handed over for treatment.

docs.t: Do donated devices need the same data erasure as sold ones?
docs.x: Yes. Art. 32 GDPR does not distinguish between buyer and recipient. Every route needs documented erasure per storage medium, or evidenced physical destruction in the case of recycling.

docs.t: Can we split a fleet between selling and donating?
docs.x: That is the most common good outcome: devices with market value are sold, devices with use value but no market are donated, broken ones are recycled. Decide the split before erasure so that every lot ends with the right record.

docs.t: IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle – how the decision gets made before the shredder does
docs.x: A hardware refresh is a procurement project. The old devices are its by-product, and their fate is usually settled where nobody asks: in the rollout plan, under "take-back of old equipment", with whichever supplier is delivering anyway. There are three routes, and they differ in money, tax, effort and evidence. The best one is rarely the same for the whole fleet. docs.t: Where the decision actually falls
docs.x: A representative survey by the German digital association Bitkom in February 2026 asked companies what they do with old devices that still work . Three quarters said they have them "properly disposed of"; a third donate; 12 per cent sell to specialist refurbishers. Multiple answers were allowed, but the headline stands: most working hardware leaves the company as waste. The reason is rarely a decision against selling or donating. It is the absence of a decision. A refresh is run around delivery, imaging, rollout and support. The old devices appear as a single line item, and by the time anyone looks at the fleet's value, a recipient's needs or the evidence the company will want later, the route is already fixed. docs.t: Three routes, three logics
docs.x: Route Logic What you get What you do not get Sale (remarketing, buy-back, lease return) Residual value is realised; the buyer wipes, refurbishes and resells Cash, an invoice, usually an erasure report A recipient you can name; a donation receipt; knowledge of where the device ends up Donation to a non-profit The device goes free of charge to an organisation that keeps using it for its original purpose A donation receipt where national law provides one, a handover record, a nameable recipient, documented re-use Cash; for depreciated devices, usually little tax benefit Recycling (take-back, e-waste treatment) The device becomes waste; materials are recovered, storage media destroyed A waste transfer record, physical destruction, low internal effort Revenue, recipient, re-use

docs.t: When a working device is not waste
docs.x: EU waste law draws the line at intent. Waste is "any substance or object which the holder discards or intends or is required to discard" (Art. 3(1) Directive 2008/98/EC). A working device that is sold or donated is not discarded: it goes to re-use , defined as any operation by which products "that are not waste are used again for the same purpose for which they were conceived" (Art. 3(13)). The waste hierarchy puts prevention and preparing for re-use ahead of recycling (Art. 4(1)). Only when a device is handed to recycling does it become waste electrical and electronic equipment. For equipment from users other than private households, Member States must ensure that the costs of collection and treatment are financed by producers for products placed on the market after 13 August 2005 (Art. 13(1) Directive 2012/19/EU); how the take-back works in practice is national.
docs.p: IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle the old fleet

docs.t: VAT: the donation is a supply, valued today
docs.x: Across the EU, giving away business assets on which input VAT was deducted is treated as a supply for consideration: the disposal of goods "free of charge" is caught by Art. 16 of the VAT Directive 2006/112/EC. The taxable amount is "the purchase price of the goods or similar goods", determined "as at the time when the application, disposal or retention takes place" (Art. 74). For a four-year-old laptop that means VAT on today's second-hand value, not on the original list price. Several Member States have relief for donations to charities, and they differ widely; our overview of VAT relief on donated goods in Europe and the EU VAT rules on in-kind donations go through them.
docs.p: IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle the old fleet

docs.t: Direct tax: national, and usually smaller than expected
docs.x: Income and corporate tax treatment of donations is not harmonised. Some countries grant a deduction, some a credit, some almost nothing. What most regimes share is that the benefit is tied to a value that, for a fully depreciated device, is small. In Germany, for example, a donation to a tax-exempt body may be withdrawn at book value (sec. 6(1) no. 4 sentence 4 EStG), which avoids a gain but limits the deductible amount to that book value plus the VAT on the withdrawal (sec. 10b(3) sentence 2 EStG). Said plainly. If you are considering donation for the tax effect, depreciated IT will disappoint you. The case for donating is the documented recipient, re-use at the top of the waste hierarchy and the data a sustainability report needs. If you need none of that and your devices still have market value, selling is often the better deal. We write this as a donation intermediary, on purpose.
docs.p: IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle the old fleet

docs.t: When selling wins on the numbers
docs.x: We do not publish flat residual-value percentages; they depend on device type, age, condition and market, and a number without a source would be invented. The structure is stable, though: Devices with a second-hand market – business notebooks and desktops of the last three to four years, current phones and tablets – usually fetch more than the effort of selling. Selling wins. Devices with use value but no market – older notebooks, monitors, docking stations, printers, peripherals – fetch little or nothing at buy-back. These are often the most useful for non-profits, whose schools, counselling services and offices run perfectly well on them. Broken or very old devices belong in recycling. A recipient who accepts them is taking your disposal problem, not a donation.
docs.p: IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle the old fleet

docs.t: Data erasure is not a variable
docs.x: All three routes share one fixed step: the data must be gone, verifiably, before the device leaves. The duty to ensure security of processing under Art. 32 GDPR does not distinguish between buyer, recipient and recycler. Sale and donation require a documented erasure procedure per storage medium; recycling replaces it with physical destruction, which also needs to be evidenced. The details are in donating corporate IT under the GDPR . The rule for this decision: fix the erasure concept before you split the fleet into lots, not after.
docs.p: IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle the old fleet

docs.t: The timeline inside the rollout plan
docs.x: T–8 weeks: inventory with type, age, condition and book value; first split into three lots; check sale candidates against documented second-hand prices. T–6 weeks: decision per lot and erasure concept per media type. T–5 weeks: buy-back quotes with contractual erasure evidence; recipients requested or matched; take-back for the recycling lot arranged. T–2 weeks: value at the time of donation documented, recipient status checked, receipts prepared where national law provides them. T0: erasure logged per device, handover signed with serial numbers – for all three lots. T+2 weeks: sale and donation booked, records filed under your national retention rules. docs.t: Office move: clear the lease, donate furniture
docs.x: In an office move the lease handover date sets the pace. What a late handover costs, why donating needs the longest lead time, and a backwards plan from twelve weeks out.

docs.t: What happens if we do not clear the office by the end of the lease?
docs.x: That depends on national law and the lease, and it is usually expensive. In Germany, for example, the landlord can claim compensation at the agreed or local market rent for the period the premises are withheld (sec. 546a(1) BGB), plus further damages. Clearing fully before the date is the safe course.

docs.t: Do we have to remove the kitchenette and partitions we installed?
docs.x: The lease almost always decides whether tenant fixtures must be removed and to what condition the premises must be returned. Clarify this before offering fixtures for donation, and ask whether the landlord or the next tenant wants to take them over.

docs.t: How early should we contact recipients for a furniture donation?
docs.x: About eight weeks before handover. Non-profits need need, space and transport at the same time, and larger volumes are split across several organisations. Collections should fall in the second-to-last week before handover, ahead of sales and the skip.

docs.t: Can we donate leased equipment?
docs.x: No. Leased and rented equipment belongs to the lessor and goes back under the contract. Mark it early in the inventory.

docs.t: Office move: handing back the premises – and what has to be gone before handover day
docs.x: In a move, the new office is the project and the old one is the problem. The old one has a date on which it must be empty, and anything still inside on that day costs money. So the question of what happens to the furniture that is not coming along is usually answered under time pressure: a skip. This guide counts backwards from handover day and shows when each decision has to fall so that donating stays a real option. Updated: 22 September 2026 Legal status: September 2026 Reading time: 7 min

docs.t: Handover day is the only fixed point
docs.x: Commercial lease law differs by Member State, but every system shares one rule: when the lease ends, the tenant returns the premises. The new site can slip, the furniture delivery can slip; the day the lease ends does not. Every decision about the old inventory that is not taken in time will be taken by that date – and that date always chooses the fastest route, not the best one. The core point. Companies do not donate too little in a move because they do not want to, but because the decision comes too late. Eight weeks before handover you have four routes. One week before, you have one.
docs.p: Office move: clear the lease, donate furniture

docs.t: What a late handover costs
docs.x: The consequences are national, but they tend to be expensive. In Germany, for example, a landlord can claim compensation for the period the premises are withheld, at the agreed rent or the local market rent (sec. 546a(1) BGB), and further damages are expressly not excluded (sec. 546a(2)) – for instance when an incoming tenant cannot move in. Other legal systems have comparable rules on holding over. Whether furniture left behind prevents a valid handover depends on the lease and the facts; we do not state a general rule. The practical risk is enough: furniture left in the space gives the landlord reason to treat the handover as incomplete and to charge for clearing it. A week of holding-over compensation for an office floor often exceeds the disposal cost of all its furniture. The uncomfortable arithmetic. The most expensive chair in a move is the one still in the office on handover day.
docs.p: Office move: clear the lease, donate furniture

docs.t: Furniture, fixtures, reinstatement: read the lease first
docs.x: Not everything in an office is inventory. Partitions, kitchenettes, hard-wired server racks, lighting and flooring are often installed by the tenant. Whether they may or must be removed, and to what condition the premises must be returned, is almost always governed by the lease; reinstatement clauses are standard, their content is not. Loose furniture (desks, chairs, cabinets): yours, free to pass on. Tenant fixtures (kitchens, partitions, lighting): check removal and reinstatement duties in the lease, and ask whether the landlord or next tenant wants to take them over. Parts of the premises : not yours, they stay. Leased and rented equipment (printers, coffee machines, IT): belongs to the lessor, goes back.
docs.p: Office move: clear the lease, donate furniture

docs.t: Four piles: move, sell, donate, dispose
docs.x: Is it coming along? Decide first; every other pile depends on it. Does it have a market? Designer furniture, young IT and conference technology can fetch money. Selling needs time for offers and collection – plan it before the donation, not after. Is it useful to someone else? Working standard furniture without market value is the typical donation. The rest is disposed of , separated as your national rules require. Electrical equipment follows its own route. The order mirrors the EU waste hierarchy, which puts prevention and preparing for re-use ahead of recycling and disposal (Art. 4(1) Directive 2008/98/EC). IT has its own chapter because erasure comes before every route: see IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle .
docs.p: Office move: clear the lease, donate furniture

docs.t: Why donating needs the longest lead time
docs.x: A waste contractor comes on call. A buyer comes when the price is right. A non-profit comes when it has need, space, transport and volunteers at the same time. That is why donations in a move fail so often – not for lack of will, but for lack of calendar. Need is specific. A counselling service needs four desks, not forty. Large volumes go to several recipients, each with its own appointment. Space is short. Many organisations cannot take stock in advance. Collection must fit their window as well as yours. Transport is the most common gap. Small associations rarely have a van. If you need handover on a fixed day, organise or coordinate transport yourself. Receipts need status checks. Where national law provides donation receipts, check the recipient's charitable status before handover, not afterwards.

docs.t: The backwards plan from twelve weeks out

docs.t: Two handover records, often confused
docs.x: Handover day produces two kinds of record. The protocol with the landlord documents the state of the premises and closes the lease. The records with recipients document what went where – and they are the basis for the donation receipt and booking, for the circular-economy data a sustainability report or customer questionnaire asks for (category, quantity, weight, recipient, treatment route; see in-kind donations and ESRS E5 ), and for the question that comes a year later: where did the old furniture actually go? What counts is your lease and the law of the Member State where the premises are. Not legal or tax advice.

docs.t: What happens if we do not clear the office by the end of the lease?
docs.x: That depends on national law and the lease, and it is usually expensive. In Germany, for example, the landlord can claim compensation at the agreed or local market rent for the period the premises are withheld (sec. 546a(1) BGB), plus further damages. Clearing fully before the date is the safe course.
docs.p: Office move: clear the lease, donate furniture

docs.t: Do we have to remove the kitchenette and partitions we installed?
docs.x: The lease almost always decides whether tenant fixtures must be removed and to what condition the premises must be returned. Clarify this before offering fixtures for donation, and ask whether the landlord or the next tenant wants to take them over.

docs.t: How early should we contact recipients for a furniture donation?
docs.x: About eight weeks before handover. Non-profits need need, space and transport at the same time, and larger volumes are split across several organisations. Collections should fall in the second-to-last week before handover, ahead of sales and the skip.

docs.t: Can we donate leased equipment?
docs.x: No. Leased and rented equipment belongs to the lessor and goes back under the contract. Mark it early in the inventory.

docs.t: Receiving in-kind donations from companies: the EU guide for nonprofits
docs.x: Since July 2026 EU companies must evidence a donation offer before destroying unsold goods. What that means for nonprofit recipients across the EU: the social economy entity test, the evidence pack, product safety, waste law, and what you may decline.

docs.t: Do we have to be a registered charity to count for a company's ESPR evidence?
docs.x: Not necessarily. Article 2(h) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296 refers to “social economy entities”, defined via Article 3(4i) of Directive 2008/98/EC as private law entities whose social or environmental purpose takes primacy over profit, which reinvest all or most of their surplus, and which have democratic or participatory governance. That is a functional test, not a tax status. Whether you can also issue a donation receipt that the donor can deduct is a separate, purely national question.

docs.t: Can a company in another EU country donate to us and still deduct it?
docs.x: Yes in principle. In Persche (C-318/07) the Court of Justice held that gifts to charitable bodies in another member state fall within free movement of capital even where they are made in kind, and that a member state may not confine the deduction to domestic bodies without letting the taxpayer show the foreign body meets the same requirements. But there is no automatic recognition (paragraph 48 of the same judgment says so expressly) and the donor carries the burden of proving comparability. Having your status certificate and statutes ready, ideally translated, is what makes that practical.

docs.t: Is there an EU-wide register of charitable recipients?
docs.x: No. Recognition is national, and the Commission's 2023 proposal for a European Cross-Border Association exists precisely because, in its own words, a very large majority of member states do not recognise associations from other member states. Some member states operate national registers; there is no EU-level equivalent.

docs.t: Are we liable under EU product safety law when we hand out donated goods for free?
docs.x: Possibly, and the honest answer is that it is not settled. Article 3(6) of the General Product Safety Regulation covers supply “whether in return for payment or free of charge”, and Article 2(3) covers used goods. The trigger is the words “in the course of a commercial activity”, which the GPSR does not define and the Commission's 2025 guidelines do not address for non-profits. The Blue Guide, which expressly does not cover the GPSR, treats non-profit activity as a case-by-case question and suggests occasional charitable supply falls outside. A regular redistribution operation or a social department store should assume it is inside and act accordingly.

docs.t: Do we need a waste permit to accept donated goods?
docs.x: Not if the goods are not waste. Waste under Article 3(1) of Directive 2008/98/EC is what the holder “discards or intends or is required to discard”. Goods handed over for continued use are re-use under Article 3(13) and therefore prevention under Article 3(12): no treatment, no permit. If items have already become waste, an operation on them is preparing for re-use under Article 3(16) and Article 23(1) requires a permit, or Article 26 registration. Because the test is the holder's intention rather than the condition of the item, get the handover documented as a transfer for continued use.

docs.t: What do we do if we cannot judge the value of a donation?
docs.x: You do not have to. For goods from business assets the value follows from the donor's own books. Ask for the figure and its basis in writing and keep it on file. Never confirm a value whose derivation you cannot follow — in most member states the liability for an incorrect receipt falls on the organisation that issued it, not on the donor, and several attach a fixed percentage of the donated amount to it.

docs.t: A company offers more than we need. What is the best answer?
docs.x: Accept the part you can place and state the quantity precisely. Partial acceptance is completely normal for companies and is recorded by quantity. If you can also name a peer organisation the remainder would suit, do — it costs you nothing and makes you the contact worth keeping. What does damage you is not replying at all: for the company's records, silence and refusal look the same, and only one of them keeps you on the list.

docs.t: Can we receive donations from outside the EU without paying duty and import VAT?
docs.x: Only with prior approval. Articles 61 to 65 of Council Regulation (EC) No 1186/2009 grant relief from import duty for basic necessities imported by charitable or philanthropic organisations approved by the competent authorities for free distribution to needy persons, and for equipment and office materials sent free of charge for operating needs; Articles 43 to 47 of Council Directive 2009/132/EC mirror this for import VAT. Alcohol, tobacco, coffee, tea and motor vehicles other than ambulances are excluded. The approval is granted nationally and must be in place before the goods arrive.

docs.x: The term is not defined in the ESPR. Article 1(1) of the delegated regulation defines it by reference to Article 3(4i) of Directive 2008/98/EC , a point inserted by Directive (EU) 2025/1892 . docs.t: Your needs profile — the single biggest lever
docs.x: The most common reason a match fails is not absence of need. It is a need nobody can see. "We are grateful for anything" reads, to a facility manager with a clearance date, as "probably not a fit", because it does not tell him whether 200 desks can land with you. Categories, and what is urgent now. Furniture, IT, textiles, tools, consumables, and which of those you are short of this quarter. An honest ceiling. "Up to 40 chairs, no more" is planning information. An open-ended answer is not. What you cannot use. Saying so costs you nothing and makes everything else you say credible. Logistics, concretely. Van or no van? Who lifts? Loading bay, lift, ramp? Up to which floor? Storage and timing. Can you buffer goods? Dry? How fast can you collect, and on which weekdays? A named person with a phone number who also answers on a Thursday afternoon. What companies actually want is neither gratit

docs.t: Product safety: free of charge is still "making available"
docs.x: This is the EU-level obligation recipients most often overlook. Under Article 3(6) of the General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988 , "making available on the market" means "any supply of a product for distribution, consumption or use on the Union market in the course of a commercial activity, whether in return for payment or free of charge ". And the regulation covers used goods. Article 2(3): "This Regulation applies to products placed or made available on the market whether new, used, repaired or reconditioned. It does not apply to products to be repaired or reconditioned prior to being used where those products are placed or made available on the market and are clearly marked as such." Whoever makes a product available while not being its manufacturer or importer is a distributor under Article 3(11), with the verification and traceability duties that follow. Where this stops be

docs.t: When goods are waste — and when they are not
docs.x: If what you accept is legally waste , an entirely different regime applies. Article 23(1) of Directive 2008/98/EC requires member states to "require any establishment or undertaking intending to carry out waste treatment to obtain a permit from the competent authority", and Article 26 requires registration of collectors, transporters, dealers and brokers who are not subject to a permit. The line is drawn by Article 3(1): waste is "any substance or object which the holder discards or intends or is required to discard". Goods handed to you while the company still intends them to be used are not waste — you are not treating waste, you are enabling re-use under Article 3(13), which is "any operation by which products or components that are not waste are used again for the same purpose for which they were conceived", and that sits inside prevention under Article 3(12), the top tier of the hie

docs.t: IT: never accept hardware without per-device erasure evidence
docs.x: Donated laptops and phones are the most valuable category and the riskiest. The GDPR does not require physical destruction — it requires a state (the data must no longer be available) and, under the accountability principle in Article 5(2), the ability to demonstrate it. But that demonstration duty belongs to whoever holds the data. Accept an unwiped device and you have accepted someone else's data protection problem. Erasure evidence per device, with the serial number — method, date, result. Not a collective note covering "40 laptops". Settle the roles before the first handover. If personal data may still be present at the point of transfer, the arrangement may amount to processing on the donor's behalf under Article 28 GDPR — that has to be agreed in advance, not discovered afterwards. Refuse devices that arrive without either. A polite sentence is enough; the donor can supply the reco

docs.t: Donation receipts and liability: national, and worth taking seriously
docs.x: Whether a donor may deduct an in-kind donation, how it is valued and who is liable if the receipt is wrong is decided by each member state. What EU law settles is only the cross-border question, and it settles it in the recipient's favour. In Persche the Court held that gifts to charitable bodies in another member state fall under free movement of capital "even if they are made in kind in the form of everyday consumer goods", and that a member state may not restrict deduction to domestic bodies "without any possibility for the taxpayer to show that a gift made to a body established in another Member State satisfies the requirements imposed by that legislation". Stauffer (C-386/04) had already established the same logic for the taxation of a foreign charitable foundation's income. Two consequences follow, and both are practical: A donor in another member state can deduct a donation to you

docs.t: If German companies donate to you: a register you can join yourself
docs.x: Germany keeps a public register of eligible donation recipients — the Zuwendungsempfängerregister under section 60b of the German Fiscal Code, maintained by the Federal Central Tax Office (BZSt). For German charities, entry is automatic. For a German donor it has become decisive: without an entry there is no deduction under section 10b of the German Income Tax Act, and with it goes a large part of the internal case for giving goods to you rather than scrapping them. Organisations based in another EU or EEA state can apply for entry themselves. The application is filed electronically through the BZSt online portal. The BZSt then examines whether your organisation meets the charitable-status requirements of German tax law. If it does, you are entered in the register and may issue your German donors a donation receipt in the official German format , which the German tax authorities recognis

docs.t: Donations from outside the EU
docs.x: Goods sent to you from a non-EU country are an import, with duty and import VAT in principle due. Two instruments provide relief, and both are conditional on prior approval : Council Regulation (EC) No 1186/2009 , Articles 61 to 65, admits free of import duties "basic necessities imported by State organisations or other charitable or philanthropic organisations approved by the competent authorities for distribution free of charge to needy persons", as well as equipment and office materials sent free of charge for operating needs. Alcohol, tobacco, coffee, tea and motor vehicles other than ambulances are excluded, and relief depends on accounts that let the authorities supervise the operation. docs.t: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy
docs.x: Large companies may no longer simply destroy unsold apparel and footwear. How returns go to non-profits, what VAT applies, and how e-commerce plugs in at returns intake.

docs.t: May we still destroy unsold clothing and footwear?
docs.x: Large companies only where a derogation under Art. 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296 applies, for example unrepairable damage or IP infringement. For usable stock the route is point (h): an offer for donation to at least three suitable social economy entities in the EU or on the company website for at least eight weeks, which was not accepted. Medium-sized companies are covered from 19 July 2030.

docs.t: Does the ban apply to electronics returns?
docs.x: Not at present: Annex VII of the ESPR currently lists clothing, clothing accessories, headgear and footwear. But the disclosure duty under Art. 24 covers consumer products generally, so discarded electronics returns still have to be reported by companies in scope.

docs.t: Is VAT due when we donate returns?
docs.x: Usually yes, where input VAT was deducted: Art. 16 of the VAT Directive treats a free disposal as a supply, and Art. 74 values it at the purchase price of similar goods at the time of the donation. For returns with limited marketability that value is reduced; for worthless goods it can fall to zero where national practice allows it, as in Germany. Fully saleable goods carry the full value.

docs.t: Do we need an IT integration to donate returns?
docs.x: No. A rule in returns grading and a weekly file with product group, quantity, condition class, weight and location are enough to start. A direct integration with shop, returns or inventory systems is an option for larger volumes.

docs.t: How do we stop donated goods from being resold?
docs.x: By contract: purpose restriction in the acceptance agreement, exclusion of resale outside recognised social channels such as social department stores, and removal of labels where needed.

docs.t: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy – and how e-commerce plugs in at the returns desk
docs.x: Returns are the part of e-commerce nobody plans for, and the part that most often ends in destruction: checked, stored, re-booked, and only months later written off. Since 19 July 2026 that last step has become a compliance question for large companies selling apparel and footwear in the EU. This guide covers what the rules require, what donating returns costs in VAT, how the routes compare – and where an online shop can connect donation to the returns process itself. docs.t: Why usable goods get destroyed
docs.x: Destruction is rarely a decision. It is where a chain of small non-decisions ends: a return that fails the resale check, a size run that no longer fits the range, last season's colours, a product line that is discontinued. Each item costs warehouse space, handling and write-down effort while it waits. When the space is needed, destruction is the fastest way to clear it – and for new goods it has often been cheaper than giving them away, because donating triggers VAT while destroying does not. The core point. The most expensive stretch in the life of an unsellable return is not the destruction but the months before it. The strongest lever is therefore not at the end of the warehouse but at the returns desk , where every item is inspected and graded anyway.
docs.p: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy

docs.t: What the destruction ban requires since July 2026
docs.x: The Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 prohibits the destruction of unsold consumer products listed in its Annex VII (Art. 25). The list currently covers clothing including headgear, clothing accessories and footwear. The ban applies to large companies since 19 July 2026 and to medium-sized companies from 19 July 2030 ; small and micro companies are exempt. Destruction remains lawful where one of the ten derogations in Art. 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296 applies – among them dangerous products, IP infringements, and damage that cannot be repaired economically. For usable stock the relevant one is point (h): the product was offered for donation, either directly to at least three suitable social economy entities in the Union or on an easily accessible page of the company's own website, for at least eight weeks , and was not accepted. Records must be kept
docs.p: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy

docs.t: The disclosure duty reaches further than the ban
docs.x: Separately, Art. 24 ESPR requires companies to disclose the number and weight of unsold consumer products they discard, the reasons and the waste treatment applied. It covers consumer products generally, not only the Annex VII scope, with exclusions such as food and medicinal products. Medium-sized companies are covered from 19 July 2030; the reporting format is set by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2 for financial years starting on or after 2 March 2027. For an online shop this means that electronics, homeware or cosmetics returns that are not banned from destruction still appear in a public disclosure – which is a reason to have a donation route for them too.

docs.t: VAT: the donation is a supply, valued by condition
docs.x: Giving away goods on which input VAT was deducted is treated as a supply for consideration (Art. 16 VAT Directive 2006/112/EC). The taxable amount is the purchase price of the goods or similar goods at the time of the donation (Art. 74). For returns that is the decisive detail: the value is set today , in today's condition. docs.x: Route Revenue Brand risk Evidence under the ban Reporting effect Sale to a stock buyer Low but positive High – grey market, uncontrolled resale None needed, no destruction Re-use, weakly documented Own outlet channel Medium Controllable Not applicable Low Donation to non-profits None; avoided storage and disposal cost Low – no market channel Carries derogation (h) and documents it Re-use, confirmed by a third party Destruction Cost None Only with a derogation Disposal – disclosed under Art. 24

docs.t: Plugging in at the returns desk
docs.x: An online shop does not need a new system to route returns to donation. It needs a rule at the point where returns are already graded, and a way to hand over what the rule sorts out. A rule in the grading step. Example: condition "limited marketability" plus product group apparel, footwear, home textiles or toys → donation lot instead of B-stock storage. Returns management sets the rule, not the person at the packing table. One collection point per site. Cartons by category and size run, filled over the week. That keeps the warehouse effort small and produces quantities a recipient can take. A file instead of an interface. Once a week, a list from the returns or inventory system: product group, quantity, condition class, weight, location. That is all matching needs. A direct integration is possible but not required to start. The confirmation back into the system. Recipient, date and quan
docs.p: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy

docs.t: Running the donation route in practice
docs.x: Offer in bundles, not items. Cartons by category and size run are acceptable to recipients; single items are not. State quantity, weight, condition, location and collection window. Choose suitable recipients and document suitability. Clothing stores for people in need, social department stores, refugee aid, family centres. An offer to an organisation that cannot use the goods counts for little as evidence. Log eight weeks. Every response with a date, including refusals and non-responses. Record partial acceptances by quantity; the derogation then covers only the remainder. Bring the records together. Handover record, donation receipt where national law provides one, quantity reconciliation, disposal record for the rest. The same numbers carry tax, the destruction-ban evidence and the disclosure.
docs.p: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy

docs.t: Brand protection
docs.x: The worry that donated goods reappear on resale platforms is legitimate and can be handled by contract: purpose restriction in the acceptance agreement, exclusion of resale outside recognised social channels such as social department stores, and removal of labels where the brand requires it and the product remains usable. Point (e) of the derogations – trade marks that cannot technically be removed – is for the rare case where none of this works. Legal status: 22 September 2026. The ESPR and its delegated and implementing acts are cited as in force on this date; VAT relief and valuation practice are national. Check the current rules in the Member States where you operate. Not legal or tax advice.
docs.p: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy

docs.t: May we still destroy unsold clothing and footwear?
docs.x: Large companies only where a derogation under Art. 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296 applies, for example unrepairable damage or IP infringement. For usable stock the route is point (h): an offer for donation to at least three suitable social economy entities in the EU or on the company website for at least eight weeks, which was not accepted. Medium-sized companies are covered from 19 July 2030.
docs.p: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy

docs.t: Does the ban apply to electronics returns?
docs.x: Not at present: Annex VII of the ESPR currently lists clothing, clothing accessories, headgear and footwear. But the disclosure duty under Art. 24 covers consumer products generally, so discarded electronics returns still have to be reported by companies in scope.
docs.p: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy

docs.t: Is VAT due when we donate returns?
docs.x: Usually yes, where input VAT was deducted: Art. 16 of the VAT Directive treats a free disposal as a supply, and Art. 74 values it at the purchase price of similar goods at the time of the donation. For returns with limited marketability that value is reduced; for worthless goods it can fall to zero where national practice allows it, as in Germany. Fully saleable goods carry the full value.
docs.p: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy

docs.t: Do we need an IT integration to donate returns?
docs.x: No. A rule in returns grading and a weekly file with product group, quantity, condition class, weight and location are enough to start. A direct integration with shop, returns or inventory systems is an option for larger volumes.
docs.p: Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy

docs.t: How do we stop donated goods from being resold?
docs.x: By contract: purpose restriction in the acceptance agreement, exclusion of resale outside recognised social channels such as social department stores, and removal of labels where needed.

docs.t: SDG 12 and R-strategies: where donations count
docs.x: In-kind donations are reuse: named in SDG target 12.5, invisible to indicator 12.5.1. How R-strategies and the waste hierarchy turn intent into evidence.

docs.t: Are the SDGs legally binding for companies?
docs.x: No. The 2030 Agenda is a UN General Assembly resolution (A/RES/70/1 of 25 September 2015) addressed to states: it creates no direct corporate obligations. Binding duties around surplus and disposal come from other sources: Article 4 of Waste Framework Directive 2008/98/EC (in Germany transposed in section 6 KrWG) and, for unsold consumer products, Article 25 of the ESPR (EU) 2024/1781.

docs.t: Does an in-kind donation count towards SDG 12?
docs.x: Yes: target 12.5 names reuse expressly as one of four routes to reducing waste generation. The official indicator 12.5.1, however, measures only the national recycling rate in tonnes; reuse does not enter it. To evidence the contribution you therefore need your own per-transaction records: category, quantity or weight, destination, recipient.

docs.t: Is donating goods recycling?
docs.x: No. In the R-framework of Potting et al. (2017), passing on functional goods is re-use (R3), not recycling (R8). Legally it sits even earlier: transfer for continued use is re-use under Article 3(13) of Directive 2008/98/EC and therefore prevention under Article 3(12), the goods never become waste. Reporting donations as recycled downgrades your own measure and describes it incorrectly.

docs.t: May we advertise as SDG-compliant?
docs.x: There is no such thing as SDG compliance, the United Nations does not certify companies and issues no label. From 27 September 2026 the EmpCo Directive (EU) 2024/825 in addition tightens the rules on environmental advertising: generic claims such as sustainable or environmentally friendly are unfair without recognised excellent environmental performance. What stays safe is specificity: quantity, destination, recipient, year.

docs.t: Which R-number does our donation have?
docs.x: Usually R3 (re-use): another organisation uses the product, in good condition, for its original function. If the product or its parts serve a different function at the recipient, it is R7 (repurpose). When citing, note that several R-lists with diverging numbering circulate; always name the source of your numbering; Potting et al. 2017 is the usual reference.

docs.t: SDG 12 and the R-strategies: where in-kind donations actually count — and why the statistics miss them
docs.x: Few frameworks are cited as often in sustainability communication as the SDGs, and few as loosely. This guide sorts it out: what the 17 goals legally are, where an in-kind donation actually counts (target 12.5), why the official SDG statistics still miss it, and how the R-strategies supply the precise vocabulary that turns good intent into evidence. Updated: 25 August 2026 Legal status: August 2026 Reading time: 9 min
docs.p: SDG 12 and R-strategies: where donations count

docs.t: Contents
docs.x: What the SDGs are, and what they are not Target 12.5: the sentence that means in-kind donations The measurement gap: reuse is statistically invisible The R-ladder: from R0 Refuse to R9 Recover Where the donation sits: R3, and sometimes R7 From framework to law: the waste hierarchy From mapping to evidence: SDG, ESRS, VSME The limits: what not to claim The SDGs are attractive for corporate communication precisely because nobody audits the reference, and that is exactly why the reference alone proves nothing. What does prove something is the combination this guide walks through: the target that names reuse, the indicator that ignores it, and the R-ladder that gives your donation its correct, defensible place.
docs.p: SDG 12 and R-strategies: where donations count

docs.t: What the SDGs are — and what they are not
docs.x: The Sustainable Development Goals come from resolution A/RES/70/1 ("Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development"), adopted by the UN General Assembly on 25 September 2015 : 17 goals, 169 targets, horizon 2030. The addressees are states , not companies. They are: a political goal system with its own set of indicators, the shared frame of reference for governments, NGOs and, increasingly, tenders and funding programmes. They are not: a law, a reporting standard or a certification basis. A General Assembly resolution is not a treaty; no direct corporate obligation follows from it. The obligations around surplus and disposal live elsewhere — in the ESPR destruction ban , in national waste law, in unfair-commercial-practices law.
docs.p: SDG 12 and R-strategies: where donations count

docs.t: Target 12.5: the sentence that means in-kind donations
docs.x: SDG 12 ("Responsible Consumption and Production") contains the target that directly concerns passing surplus on. Target 12.5 reads: "By 2030, substantially reduce waste generation through prevention, reduction, recycling and reuse ." Reuse stands there expressly, on equal footing with recycling. An in-kind donation of functional goods (office furniture, IT, returns, excess stock) is exactly that: a product keeps its function and merely changes its user. A company that donates instead of discarding is not acting "in the spirit" of the 2030 Agenda; it is acting along the literal wording of 12.5.
docs.p: SDG 12 and R-strategies: where donations count

docs.t: The measurement gap: reuse is statistically invisible
docs.x: Now the uncomfortable half of the truth. Every target has official indicators against which UN statistics measure progress. For 12.5 there is exactly one: indicator 12.5.1, "National recycling rate, tons of material recycled" . It counts recycling, composting and anaerobic digestion. Reuse is not recorded. The result is a paradox worth knowing before you put SDG references into a report: the target names four routes, the indicator measures one. A company that passes a thousand pieces of furniture to nonprofit recipients for continued use improves its country’s SDG statistics by exactly zero tonnes. Had it shredded the same furniture for material recovery, the tonnage would have counted as recycling, although that is the environmentally worse tier. What follows from this. The SDG indicator set is unusable as evidence of reuse, not because donating does not count, but because it is not cou
docs.p: SDG 12 and R-strategies: where donations count

docs.t: The R-ladder: from R0 Refuse to R9 Recover
docs.x: Where the SDGs supply the why , the R-strategies supply the how , a ranking of circularity strategies ordered by value retention. The most cited version is by Potting, Hekkert, Worrell and Hanemaaijer (2017) , published by the Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (PBL): ten strategies from R0 to R9 in three groups. The ground rule: the lower the number, the higher the value retention. Strategy Core Relation to the donation R0 Refuse Make the product redundant, avoid raw material use Acts before the surplus exists — prevents it rather than recovering it R1 Rethink Intensify use (sharing, multifunctional design) R2 Reduce Resource efficiency in design and manufacture R3 Re-use Continued use of an intact product by another user, same function The in-kind donation of functional goods — this exact definition R4 Repair Repair defects, retain function Upstream steps: turn defective stock
docs.p: SDG 12 and R-strategies: where donations count

docs.t: Where the donation sits: R3 — and sometimes R7
docs.x: The definition of R3 re-use (continued use of a product in good condition by another user, in its original function) describes an in-kind donation of functional goods word for word. The desk stays a desk, the laptop stays a laptop; only the user changes. If the recipient uses the product or its parts for a different purpose, it is R7 repurpose — also a high-retention strategy, two tiers above recycling. Which yields the most important distinction in this guide: donating is not recycling. Reporting donated furniture as "recycled" makes two mistakes at once: it downgrades your own measure in the value hierarchy, and it describes it incorrectly, because recycling presupposes the material processing of waste. Donated goods, precisely, never become waste.
docs.p: SDG 12 and R-strategies: where donations count

docs.t: From framework to law: the waste hierarchy
docs.x: The R-ladder is analysis, not law. But it has a legal mirror: the five-tier waste hierarchy in Article 4(1) of Waste Framework Directive 2008/98/EC — (a) prevention, (b) preparing for re-use, (c) recycling, (d) other recovery, (e) disposal — transposed in Germany in section 6 of the Kreislaufwirtschaftsgesetz, which also gives priority to the option that best protects human health and the environment across the whole life cycle. The point that is almost always missed in practice: transferring functional goods for continued use is re-use within the meaning of Article 3(13) and therefore prevention under Article 3(12): tier (a), before the goods ever become waste. "Preparing for re-use" on tier (b), by contrast, covers only items that have already become waste. A timely donation keeps the surplus out of the waste regime altogether — with the documentation consequences described in the guid
docs.p: SDG 12 and R-strategies: where donations count

docs.t: From mapping to evidence: SDG, ESRS, VSME
docs.x: This separates the three levels that get mixed constantly in practice: Level Frame Function Communication SDG mapping Shows which goals your actions serve — legitimate and useful, as long as every mapping is concretely evidenced: "Our in-kind donations contribute to 12.5: in 2026, X kg were transferred for reuse." Evidence ESRS E5 / VS B7 The auditable material flow per transaction — covered for reporting undertakings in the guide to ESRS E5 , including the Voluntary Standard’s disclosure B7 for smaller companies. Operations R-strategies The decision logic before every disposal: check R3 first (usable by someone else?), then R4–R7 (repairable, repurposable?), only then R8. As a process rule: "No container before the reuse check is documented." Follow that order and the SDG communication comes free: it is then merely the summary of what the evidence dataset already proves, instead of a se

docs.t: The limits: what not to claim
docs.x: From 27 September 2026 environmental claims face a considerably stricter frame: the EmpCo Directive (EU) 2024/825 (transposition deadline 27 March 2026, national rules applying from 27 September 2026) classes generic environmental claims such as "environmentally friendly", "green" or "sustainable" without recognised excellent environmental performance as unfair commercial practices, as is advertising with legal requirements as if they were distinctive features. Check the transposition status in your member state before a campaign. No "SDG-compliant", no "SDG-certified": the United Nations does not certify companies. There is no compliance to invoke — only the evidenced, specific contribution. No invented rates: a "reuse rate" without a documented denominator is contestable. Report absolute, evidenced quantities. No CO₂ figures without methodology: avoided emissions from reuse can be calc

docs.t: Store closure: donating shop fittings
docs.x: When a store closes, the fittings are yours and the stock is a different matter. What tills, refrigeration and the lease require, and which fittings non-profits can use.

docs.t: May we donate the fittings of a closed store?
docs.x: Yes, as far as they belong to you: loose fittings and tenant fit-out that does not have to be removed or handed over to the landlord. Rented or leased items such as POS systems go back to the provider. The donation is a disposal of business assets, with VAT and direct-tax treatment under national rules.

docs.t: What do we need to do with the till before it is passed on?
docs.x: Complete the decommissioning duties for fiscal recording systems in your Member State – in Germany, notifying the tax office within one month (sec. 146a(4) AO) – and secure the transaction data for the retention period. Then erase every storage medium with a log, as for any IT donation.

docs.t: Can refrigerated counters be donated to a food bank?
docs.x: Plug-in units usually can, if power, space, door width and transport fit at the recipient. Units on a central system need the refrigerant recovered by certified personnel before decommissioning (Art. 8 Regulation (EU) 2024/573) and are rarely useful as donations.

docs.t: Does the EU destruction ban apply to shop fittings?
docs.x: No. Art. 25 of the Ecodesign Regulation concerns unsold consumer products, currently apparel, clothing accessories and footwear held by large companies. Shop fittings are business equipment. For them the waste hierarchy applies, which ranks re-use above recycling, but there is no ban.

docs.t: Store closure: donating the shop fittings – and what has to happen to shelving, tills and refrigeration first
docs.x: When a store closes, everything revolves around the stock: clearance sales, return transport, leftovers. The fittings are what remains once the last customer has left: shelving, counters, checkouts, lighting, refrigeration, fitting rooms, the back office. They are almost always business equipment, almost never goods for resale, and that is exactly why they follow different rules from the stock. This guide separates the two and shows what can be donated and what has to be done first. Updated: 22 September 2026 Legal status: September 2026 Reading time: 8 min

docs.t: Two inventories, two sets of rules
docs.x: A closing store holds two fundamentally different things. The stock is inventory held for sale, with its own rules on destruction, returns and donation. The fittings are fixed assets or low-value equipment, depreciated over years and used in the business. Mixing them leads to the wrong questions – about the destruction ban for shelving, or about donation relief for leftover stock. The core point. Fittings are the part of a store closure where donating is easiest and rarest. Easiest, because they are business equipment and the rules are the same as for an office clearance. Rarest, because nobody deals with them until the stock is gone – and by then handover day has arrived.
docs.p: Store closure: donating shop fittings

docs.t: The stock: why it is not the subject here
docs.x: Stock has its own rules. Donating new goods is a supply for VAT purposes (Art. 16 VAT Directive), with the taxable amount set at the purchase price at the time of the donation (Art. 74). For unsold apparel, clothing accessories and footwear, large companies have been subject to the EU destruction ban with a documented donation offer since July 2026 (Art. 25 Regulation (EU) 2024/1781; see the EU destruction ban 2026 ). Stock and fittings have different owners in the organisation, different recipients and different records. Make the fittings a lot of their own in the closure plan, not the remainder after the clearance sale.

docs.t: A till is not furniture
docs.x: A point-of-sale system is a recording system for tax purposes, and most Member States attach duties to it: registration, fiscal devices, retention of transaction data. Those duties usually extend to decommissioning. In Germany, for example, taking an electronic recording system out of service must be notified to the tax office within one month (sec. 146a(4) AO). The data must be secured for the statutory retention period before any device is wiped and passed on; that is a job for your POS provider. After that, till PCs, scanners and printers are IT like any other: erasure per storage medium with a log (Art. 32 GDPR), then donation, sale or recycling per lot, as in IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle . Rented or leased POS systems go back to the provider.

docs.t: Refrigeration: plug-in or central system
docs.x: Refrigerated counters and freezers are often the most valuable thing a closing store can give a food bank. Whether they can be passed on depends on one technical question: is the unit self-contained, or connected to a central refrigeration plant? Plug-in units have a sealed circuit and can be removed, moved and reconnected elsewhere. Units on a central system have refrigerant lines running to a shared compressor; disconnecting them opens the circuit. Then the F-gas Regulation applies: operators of equipment containing fluorinated greenhouse gases "shall ensure that fluorinated greenhouse gases are recovered from that equipment prior to its decommissioning" (Art. 8(1) Regulation (EU) 2024/573), by certified natural persons (Art. 8(2) with Art. 10). A central system is a job for a refrigeration contractor, not a donation pickup – and rarely useful as a donation, because the recipient would

docs.t: Fit-out, lease and handover day
docs.x: Retail space is almost always leased, and fittings are often installed by the tenant. The same logic as in an office move applies, with more fixtures: the premises must be returned when the lease ends, late return is usually expensive, and whether fit-out must be removed is a question for the lease. Two consequences for donating: an incoming tenant may want to take over parts of the fit-out, which is often the simplest route; and handover day sets the order – recipients collect first, strip-out follows. The backwards plan is in Office move: handing back the premises ; it applies to a shop floor just as well.
docs.p: Store closure: donating shop fittings

docs.t: When the closure is an insolvency
docs.x: If the store closes in insolvency proceedings, the decisive question changes from what can be donated to who may decide. In most Member States the power to dispose of the estate passes to an insolvency practitioner, whose duty is to realise it for the creditors. In Germany, for example, the right of disposal passes to the administrator when proceedings open (sec. 80(1) InsO), who must then realise the estate without delay (sec. 159 InsO). Donation is not excluded: for fittings that fetch nothing and would cost the estate money to strip out and dispose of, a non-profit that collects them itself can be the best economic result for the estate. But the decision, and the consent to every handover, lies with the practitioner.
docs.p: Store closure: donating shop fittings

docs.t: Ten stores, ten regions
docs.x: Closing several stores at once produces not one large donation lot but many small ones, in different places on different dates. Recipients are local: a food bank in one town will not collect in another, and the density of non-profits varies strongly by region. Chains usually have the same fit-out everywhere, so an inventory template per store format and a standard request to recipients save most of the work. For the tax file and the sustainability report, what counts in the end is the total – categories, quantities, recipients and treatment route, recorded per store and consolidated centrally ( in-kind donations and ESRS E5 ). Legal status: 22 September 2026. VAT, fiscal till rules, lease law and insolvency law are national; German provisions are cited as examples. For refrigeration systems, rely on the assessment of a certified contractor. Not legal or tax advice.

docs.t: May we donate the fittings of a closed store?
docs.x: Yes, as far as they belong to you: loose fittings and tenant fit-out that does not have to be removed or handed over to the landlord. Rented or leased items such as POS systems go back to the provider. The donation is a disposal of business assets, with VAT and direct-tax treatment under national rules.

docs.t: What do we need to do with the till before it is passed on?
docs.x: Complete the decommissioning duties for fiscal recording systems in your Member State – in Germany, notifying the tax office within one month (sec. 146a(4) AO) – and secure the transaction data for the retention period. Then erase every storage medium with a log, as for any IT donation.
docs.p: Store closure: donating shop fittings

docs.t: Can refrigerated counters be donated to a food bank?
docs.x: Plug-in units usually can, if power, space, door width and transport fit at the recipient. Units on a central system need the refrigerant recovered by certified personnel before decommissioning (Art. 8 Regulation (EU) 2024/573) and are rarely useful as donations.

docs.t: Does the EU destruction ban apply to shop fittings?
docs.x: No. Art. 25 of the Ecodesign Regulation concerns unsold consumer products, currently apparel, clothing accessories and footwear held by large companies. Shop fittings are business equipment. For them the waste hierarchy applies, which ranks re-use above recycling, but there is no ban.

docs.t: Where donating is VAT-free in Europe - country by country
docs.x: France, Belgium, Germany and the UK compared: which countries relieve VAT on donated goods, why every EU relief targets new unsold merchandise rather than used business assets, and what changed in the UK on 1 April 2026.

docs.t: Is there any EU country where donating used business assets is VAT-free?
docs.x: Not that we could verify as of August 2026. France's Article 273 septies D CGI covers new unsold goods only, Belgium's regime covers food and essential non-food necessities, and Germany's BMF letter of 18 March 2021 only reduces the valuation for goods of limited marketability. Used operating assets - retired IT, furniture, equipment - remain a deemed supply under Article 16 of the VAT Directive in every member state we checked.

docs.t: What VAT relief did the UK introduce on 1 April 2026?
docs.x: A new exception to the deemed-supply rules in Schedule 4 of the VAT Act 1994, with zero-rating via Item 2, Group 15, Schedule 8: business donations of goods to registered charities carry no VAT, up to 100 pounds per item, or 200 pounds for laptops, mobile phones, furniture and white goods. Second-hand goods are expressly covered; excise goods are excluded and the donor needs a certification from the charity.

docs.t: Does France's AGEC relief apply to used equipment?
docs.x: No. Article 273 septies D of the Code general des impots, inserted by the AGEC law 2020-105, waives the VAT adjustment only for donated unsold new goods (invendus neufs) given to eligible bodies with a donation certificate. Used business assets are outside its scope.

docs.t: Why is destroying goods VAT-free when donating is not?
docs.x: Because VAT taxes supplies. A donation is a deemed supply under Article 16 of Directive 2006/112/EC where input VAT was deducted; destruction is not a supply to anyone, so no VAT arises. The result is a structural asymmetry: the tax system prices the donation and leaves the skip free.

docs.t: How should an EU company value a donation of used goods?
docs.x: Article 74 of the VAT Directive sets the taxable amount at the purchase price of the goods or of similar goods, determined at the time of the disposal - meaning the market price of equivalent used goods on the donation date, not the original invoice price. Documented market comparables with source and date are the practical evidence.

docs.t: Where donating beats destroying: the state of VAT relief for donated goods across Europe
docs.x: France, Belgium and now the UK have passed relief laws. Read the legal texts and one pattern emerges: almost everything covers new unsold merchandise — and almost nothing covers the used assets companies actually donate. Updated: 16 October 2026 Legal status: October 2026 Reading time: 9 min
docs.p: Where donating is VAT-free in Europe - country by country

docs.t: Contents
docs.x: The baseline: donating is a taxable supply by default The map: who relieves what The pattern: relief follows retail, not reuse What the UK changed — and why it matters beyond the UK What companies inside the EU can do today Ask why more European companies do not donate their surplus, and the answer is usually one sentence from finance: destroying stock costs nothing in VAT, donating it can. Several countries have passed relief laws in response — France, Belgium, and most recently the United Kingdom. Read the actual legal texts, though, and a pattern appears that almost nobody spells out: nearly every relief in Europe is written for new, unsold merchandise or food. The goods companies actually retire — used laptops, desks, chairs, equipment — fall through the gap in every EU member state we checked. The one-line version: Europe’s VAT reliefs reward retailers for donating what they could n
docs.p: Where donating is VAT-free in Europe - country by country

docs.t: The baseline: donating is a taxable supply by default
docs.x: The starting position is harmonised across all 27 member states. Under Article 16 of the VAT Directive 2006/112/EC , giving away business goods free of charge is treated as a supply for consideration where input VAT on those goods was wholly or partly deducted. Article 74 sets the taxable amount: the purchase price of the goods or of similar goods , determined at the time when the disposal takes place . Destruction, by contrast, is not a supply to anyone — no VAT arises. That asymmetry is the whole problem: the tax system prices generosity and leaves waste free. How the valuation works in practice, and why the disposal-date wording is your strongest lever, is covered in our guide to VAT and tax on in-kind donations in the EU . This page asks a different question: where has the default actually been switched off — and for which goods?
docs.p: Where donating is VAT-free in Europe - country by country

docs.t: The map: who relieves what
docs.x: Country Relief Covers Used business assets? France No deemed-supply adjustment for donated unsold goods (Art. 273 septies D CGI, inserted by the AGEC law 2020-105) New unsold goods ( invendus neufs ) donated to eligible bodies, with a donation certificate No — the provision is expressly limited to new goods Belgium Donation regime in Art. 12 §1 of the VAT Code, extended in 2019 beyond food; administrative detail in Circulars 2020/C/58 and 2020/C/104 Food and essential non-food goods ( biens de première nécessité ) that can no longer be sold in normal commerce No — unsold necessities, not retired equipment Germany No statutory relief. The Federal Ministry of Finance letter of 18 March 2021 allows a reduced — down to zero — valuation Only goods of limited marketability (damaged, near expiry, deep-discount stock) No — ordinary used assets are valued at replacement cost

docs.t: The pattern: relief follows retail, not reuse
docs.x: Look at what the reliefs have in common. France’s Article 273 septies D was written into the anti-waste law AGEC — its target is retailers destroying unsold inventory. Belgium’s regime speaks of goods that can no longer be sold in normal commerce . Germany’s administrative concession turns on marketability. All three answer the same question: what do we do about unsold merchandise? But unsold merchandise is not what most companies have. A software firm, a bank, an engineering office — their surplus is used operating assets : the laptop fleet after a refresh, 200 desks after a move, monitors, tools, shelving. For that category there is no relief anywhere in the EU. The donation is a deemed supply at the replacement cost of equivalent used goods, while the skip remains VAT-free. Since 19 July 2026 this asymmetry has a second edge. The EU destruction ban requires large companies to evidence
docs.p: Where donating is VAT-free in Europe - country by country

docs.t: What the UK changed — and why it matters beyond the UK
docs.x: From 1 April 2026 , a UK business donating goods to a registered charity no longer accounts for VAT on the gift, provided the charity uses the goods in its activities or passes them on — and the per-item value stays within £100, or £200 for the categories where used corporate assets actually live: laptops, phones, furniture, white goods. The relief expressly covers second-hand goods. The design is instructive for EU policymakers precisely because of those caps: they keep the relief targeted at genuine surplus rather than opening a valuation loophole, while finally covering the asset classes that corporate donations are made of. A used £180 laptop qualifies; a luxury watch does not.
docs.p: Where donating is VAT-free in Europe - country by country

docs.t: What companies inside the EU can do today
docs.x: Until the law changes, the working levers are the ones the Directive itself provides. First, value at the disposal date : Article 74 prices the goods as they are on the day you give them away — a five-year-old desk at its used-market price, not its invoice price. Second, document the basis : market comparables for equivalent used goods, with source and date. Third, if you hold new unsold merchandise in France or Belgium, use the national regimes that exist — they are conditional on certificates and eligible recipients, but they are real. And fourth, weigh the full ledger: disposal costs avoided, the deduction where national law grants one, and the compliance value of an evidenced donation offer under the destruction ban. docs.x: sur.plus documents each donation as a transaction: a handover record per match, valuation evidence with source and timestamp for the Article 74 basis, and the recipient’s confirmation — the file your tax adviser and, since the destruction ban, your compliance team both need. What it is not: tax advice, and not a way around national law. Whether a relief applies to your goods in your member state is a question for your adviser there. docs.t: 2. What sur.plus does, and does not do
docs.x: sur.plus is an intermediation platform. We match surplus goods you no longer need with verified recipients, coordinate the handover, and generate the documentation for it. We never take ownership of your goods. The transfer is direct between you and the recipient. sur.plus is not a party to it, does not buy, sell, store or transport the goods, and does not act as your agent. Title, risk and any warranty pass directly between you and the recipient. Handover, passing of risk and transport. The risk of accidental loss or deterioration passes when the goods are handed over to the recipient or to a person acting on its behalf; where you organise transport, on delivery to the recipient. We set up an account in the application once the relevant area has been enabled for corporate customers; until then, your contact at sur.plus is your access. Matching and handover. Matching is coordinated by people: we check your details, approach verified recipients, agree quantities, dates and transport with both sides and accompany the handover. Offers, commitments and handover dates are recorded in text form, usually by e-mail. Documentation. docs.x: Registration is free and opens the platform: you can browse what verified recipients currently need, including which organisation posted each need. docs.t: 4. Connections stay on the platform
docs.x: Recipient contact details are disclosed to you for the purpose of completing a specific match. You agree not to use them to arrange comparable transfers with that recipient outside sur.plus for the duration of your plan and 12 months after, and not to pass them to third parties. This is what keeps the network free for non-profits: they are not the product, and they are not a lead list. Nothing here restricts a relationship you already had with a recipient before sur.plus introduced you, or contact the recipient initiates for other purposes.

docs.t: 5. What we ask of you
docs.x: Only list goods you own and are entitled to dispose of, that are usable for their purpose, and that are lawful to transfer. Leased or rented items and items subject to retention of title are not among them. Do not list recalled, unsafe, expired or sanctioned items. Describe condition accurately and name known defects: a recipient plans around it, the donation receipt is based on it, and a named defect is not a concealed one. Identity of the goods. State manufacturer, model and, where available, serial or batch number per line item. This is the basis of the donation receipt, enables recall checks and allows you to name the manufacturer in the event of a product-related damage claim (§ 4(3) ProdHaftG). Data and licences. Do not list devices that still hold personal data or that are enrolled in device management or protected by an activation lock. Wiping IT hardware is your responsibility u

docs.t: 6. Discounted transfer to small businesses and private individuals
docs.x: Recipients are usually tax-privileged organisations and public or church-run bodies. Small businesses and private individuals running a public-benefit project may also receive surplus. The usual route is a discounted transfer for a symbolic price against an invoice, because an outright gift to these groups is not a deductible donation and may count as taxable income for the recipient. An outright gift remains possible if you expressly want that; it then carries no donation effect. You choose the route in the offer. For a paid transfer, the sale is concluded directly between you and the recipient. sur.plus intermediates, is not the seller and does not become a party to the sale. You are the seller, with the obligations that follow. The contract is not concluded through the application. The application makes the introduction, displays your offer and documents the handover.
